articles.title: Hinojosa shows up for proposed debate. Abbott is more than 200 miles away
articles.summary: Her challenge named a time and a place. His schedule put him in Tyler. Voters start casting ballots Monday without seeing them together.
articles.body:
Democratic nominee Gina Hinojosa challenged Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to a debate at the Governor's Mansion in Austin, though Abbott never publicly agreed to participate.

Hinojosa went to the Governor's Mansion on Oct. 15 and criticized Abbott for not being there. At the time, Abbott was more than 200 miles away in Tyler for a roundtable with law enforcement.

"I promised that I would show up for her for a debate, to answer questions," Hinojosa said in Austin. "I am happy to answer questions. The governor is hiding."

Abbott was in Tyler, east of Dallas, meeting with local sheriffs, law enforcement, and lawmakers that day about his public safety agenda.

When asked whether he would debate Hinojosa at a press conference in Tyler after his roundtable, Abbott said he preferred talking directly to voters in Texas communities, which he said had a proven track record.

"When I go to each of those communities, I learn something new," Abbott said in Tyler. "I am a better governor, I am a better governor candidate by talking to those people."

These latest events in the gubernatorial race come as Hinojosa is within striking distance of Abbott, either trailing by single digits in the summer or, in recent polls, leading Abbott — within the poll's margin of error.

An Oct. 14 Marist poll showed Abbott leading Hinojosa 49% to 45% among likely voters — within the poll's margin of error, making the race a statistical tie. Among registered voters, the two gubernatorial candidates are separated by 1 point.

Early voting starts in Texas on Oct. 19 and ends Oct. 30. Election Day is Nov. 3.

Marist poll (Oct. 14) — Abbott 49%, Hinojosa 45%

UT/Texas Politics Project (Oct. 13) — Hinojosa 49%, Abbott 48%

ReconMR (Oct. 13 ) — Abbott 48%, Hinojosa 47%

UMass Lowell (Oct. 8) — Abbott 48%, Hinojosa 44%.

YouGov poll (Oct. 6 ) — Hinojosa 48%, Abbott 47%.

The New York Times (Oct. 3) — Hinojosa 49%, Abbott 46%.

Fox News (Oct. 1) — Abbott 52%, Hinojosa 47%.

Mateo Rosiles is the Texas Connect reporter for USA TODAY and its regional papers in Texas, based in Austin. Got a news tip for him? Email him at mrosiles@usatodayco.com.

articles.title: Trump wants the midterms to be all about himself. Judging by the ads, Democrats are happy to oblige
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump says he wants voters to pretend that he's on the ballot in this year's midterm elections.His rivals are doing their be...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump says he wants voters to pretend that he's on the ballot in this year's midterm elections .

His rivals are doing their best to help his case.

Democratic candidates and their allies have spent more than $163 million since Sept. 1 on television advertising that mentions the Republican president, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, which charts media spending.

That includes airing ads that reference Trump on broadcast, cable and streaming nearly 180,000 times, the data shows. Republicans, meanwhile, have run ads that talk about the president just 16,000 times, at an estimated cost of $11 million, over the same period.

It's a noticeable silence about the party's dominant yet unpopular leader.

Many of the Democrats' ads accuse Republican opponents of siding with the president over voters, particularly on issues like tariffs and the Iran war, which they blame for jacking up costs.

The ads include one from the campaign of Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is running for reelection and has spent nearly $3 million on a Trump-focused ad attacking his rival, Rep. Mike Collins, for his close relationship with the president.

"Mike Collins voted for Trump's war in Iran, sending gas prices through the roof. He voted for Trump's tariffs, sending grocery prices soaring. And Mike Collins voted with Trump to double health insurance premiums for more than a million Georgians," it says. "Mike Collins sides with Donald Trump and makes you pay more."

Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said Democratic messaging reflected the party's hollowness instead of its strength.

"Democrats are lighting money on fire talking about President Trump because they have no agenda other than investigation, obstruction and impeachment," she said. "Trump Derangement Syndrome isn't a policy platform, it's a $160 million way of saying you have nothing to offer to the American people."

Democrats link Trump and his allies to economic woes

Another ad from the House Majority PAC, a super PAC dedicated to electing Democrats to the House, opens with a middle-aged woman standing over her kitchen stove and talking about how her family is "barely getting by" before she expresses her disappointment in Pennsylvania Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who is one of Republicans' vulnerable incumbents .

"He used to be independent. But now it seems like he's in lockstep with Donald Trump. It really bothers me," she says, adding, "Congressman Fitzpatrick is not for us anymore."

Indeed, all the Democratic ads that have aired in Pennsylvania's tightly contested 1st Congressional District since Sept. 1 have mentioned Trump, even though Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval.

All four of the ads talking about Trump have aired a combined 2,000 times in that period, the AdImpact data shows. Fitzpatrick is being challenged by Democrat Bob Harvie, a county commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.

Democratic strategists say the messaging reflects the sentiment of voters.

"Every single poll and every single focus group shows affordability to be voters' number one issue, and they specifically point to corrupt politicians as being responsible for driving up prices," said House Majority PAC spokesperson Katarina Flicker.

Republican ads back away from the president

Out of dozens of issue categories tracked by AdImpact, the analysis found that Trump was the fourth most common issue mentioned by Democrats in House and Senate races' final stretch. It was topped only by healthcare, taxes and accusations about opponents being beholden to special interests.

For Republicans in the same races, Trump-themed ads clocked in at number 33, by comparison. The top issues in their ads were taxes and crime.

Idaho Republican Senator Jim Risch tells viewers he "fought alongside President Trump to pass the biggest tax cuts for working families in American history."

Overall in the race's final stretch since Sept. 1, Democrats have spent or plan to spend $1.8 billion in ads across all federal, state and local elections. Republicans have spent or reserved $2.2 billion nationwide.

Republican strategist Alex Conant said Democrats are banking on Trump motivating their base to vote, an approach they've routinely used over the last decade.

"Democrats want this election to be a referendum on Trump. They want to equate a vote for a Republican candidate to a vote for Trump," he said.

For Conant's party, it's a different calculus.

"We have a ton of money and we're throwing every kind of message on the wall to see what sticks," he said. "There's not a cookie-cutter Republican ad this year. Whereas the Democratic ads are pretty obvious."

articles.title: Why is France Burning?
articles.summary: The postwar model of a welfare state run by civil servants charged with modernizing the economy, tempering market forces and defining the common good has run...
articles.body:
The French like to take to the streets, and they do it often.

On Sept. 17, students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry, a rather underprivileged high school in the Paris suburb of Créteil, erupted in protest over the abysmal conditions of their institution: chronic shortfall of teachers, poor facilities, long declining quality of education. Two weeks later, a wave of protests had swept cities across France. Students from hundreds of schools and scores of universities joined the protests , backed by their parents, teachers, and trade unions. More than 160,000 students and trade unionists protested across France on Tuesday in the third week of demonstrations.

France has never seen so many violent incidents in a movement made up largely of high school students. So far, over 200 students , 85 school staff, and 700 police officers have been injured in clashes across the country. Protesters have broken into schools and, in some cases, set fire to occupied or blockaded buildings. On Oct. 5, a 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off by a police grenade during a protest in Lens in northern France, an incident that crystallized the heavy-handed response authorities had adopted from the earliest days of the protest. More than 6,000 protesters have been arrested , most of them minors, and later released without charge.

The protests erupted after nearly a decade of Macronisme , the right-of-center, top-down governing style that President Emmanuel Macron of France incarnates. And they express a broader discontent: anger over disparities in school quality, university admissions decisions, and latent racial discrimination, and a sense among young people that those in power were not listening to them, that the country offered them little hope for the future.

The protests are also occurring amid a wider crisis of political confidence in the country. France is holding its presidential elections in April 2027, and the far-right and far-left are leading the opinion polls. The frontrunner is Marine Le Pen, who has worked for years to make her far-right party, the National Rally, more electable while campaigning on immigration, crime, and denunciation of an out-of-touch political class. Her party is already the largest opposition party in parliament, and a snap legislative election following the presidential vote could entrench it further.

On the other side is Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed , a far-left party, who is promising a sweeping redistribution of power and resources toward the working class. Both have built much of their appeal on opposition to the political establishment, the promise to wish away budget constraints, and deep hostility toward the European Union.

If France today feels like it is at a crossroads, it is because it is. The postwar model of a large welfare and regulatory state, run by a class of civil servants charged with modernizing the economy, tempering market forces and defining the common good, has run its course.

France now runs one of Europe's largest budget deficits: its public debt stands at 119.3 % of GDP and is expected to rise next year. Fears of a crippling financial crisis are growing. Borrowing costs have risen so high that France is drawing comparisons with Greece , whose debt crisis in 2010 threatened the survival of the Eurozone. And with economic growth stagnating, there is no easy way out.

If anything, France would need to spend more: on defense, as Russia grows more threatening, the war in Ukraine continues, and the United States retreats from its traditional role as Europe's security guarantor; on new technologies, as the country that once produced Concorde and high-speed trains now trails in high-tech innovation and AI; on strained public services, from schools to hospitals to neglected neighborhoods; and on infrastructure capable of withstanding the growing effects of climate change.

Successive French governments have promised to turn things around and allow for these badly needed investments in the country's future, but none has succeeded.

The French malaise goes deeper. Inequality has been one of the students' central grievances. They are not wrong. As in many countries, economic inequalities in France have widened over the past two decades under the combined effects of globalization, industrial decline, and the growing concentration of inherited wealth.

In Capital in the Twenty-First Century , the French economist Thomas Piketty showed how wealth perpetuates across generations and widens the divide between those who own capital and everyone else. This concentration of wealth and power remains deeply resented: for many , President Macron's original sin is still his brief stint at the Rothschild investment bank before entering politics.

But the most injurious form of inequality lies elsewhere: in the power of France's national meritocratic myth, which holds that people broadly owe their social position largely to their academic performance. At the top of that system sit the highly competitive grandes écoles , the elite institutions of higher education that have produced leaders in politics, culture, and business.

What makes the myth so corrosive is not that academic achievement goes unrewarded but that it remains a pretty reliable path to better jobs, higher status, and positions of power. In such a system, students from underfunded public schools face a profound disadvantage compared with peers who attend better-resourced schools and whose better-educated parents know how to navigate the system.

Private schools offer another route, but are still frowned upon as a way to buy an advantage. It is no surprise that the protests broke out in Créteil, a working-class suburb just outside Paris, where schools are chronically under-resourced.

Racial and geographic discrimination also contribute to the crisis of France. The collection of ethno-racial statistics is prohibited by French law; it is a laudable restriction in principle but problematic in practice. Visible minorities remain vastly underrepresented among France's political and business elites.

Families with immigrant backgrounds, many with roots in African and Asian countries once colonized by France, are disproportionately concentrated on urban peripheries, where jobs are scarce and residents often face discrimination from employers elsewhere.

Islamophobia has also grown over the last decade amid conflicts in the Middle East and a string of Islamist-inspired terrorist attacks. Rhetoric once largely confined to the far right has seeped into the mainstream right, where calls for "order" and "security" often carry an anti-immigrant charge. Macron's references to the " decivilization " of some young people and former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau's description of immigrants' participation in the protests that followed the police killing of a teenager in 2023 as a " regression towards ethnic origins " are emblematic of that shift.

There is another problem with France's meritocratic ideal: Paris. Political power, economic opportunity, cultural prestige, and elite education remain extraordinarily concentrated in the capital. The result is a deep economic divide between Paris and the rest of the country and an elite that lives largely among its own, surrounded by people with similar educations, careers, and assumptions, and cut off from much of the country.

The Yellow Vest revolt of 2018 to 2019 was an earlier social explosion of precisely that resentment. It is hardly surprising that students are denouncing the unequal distribution of resources between Paris and the rest of the country, or that the protests began in Créteil, close enough to the capital for the contrast to be impossible to miss.

When students from my own former school, the elite Lycée Henri-IV, where I was a rather poor student, joined the movement in its third week, I noticed how carefully they described themselves as protesting "in solidarity" with less privileged schools. They knew which side of the divide they were on. So much for meritocracy.

Where does this leave France? With the presidential elections approaching next April, political parties are scrambling to position themselves in relation to a protest movement that has shown no sign of abating. On Oct. 6, more than a quarter-million people took to the streets as high school students were joined by university students, teachers, parents and trade unions. An even wider " national day of protest " is planned for Oct. 17.

Both familiar and new dynamics will shape the election. The familiar one is the runoff dilemma: voters may once again be asked to support a candidate from the opposite political camp simply to prevent Le Pen from reaching the Élysée. Le Pen made the runoff in both 2017 and 2022 and is leading the polls by a large margin. This time, however, the field trailing her is unusually fragmented. Two former prime ministers under Macron, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, are in the race; Philippe is competing with Mélenchon for second place, while Attal trails both.

Whatever the outcome, the presidential vote may resolve little. A president from the far-right National Rally could find herself governing without a stable parliamentary majority or broad support among the public or within the civil service. A compromise candidate from the center or left could face the same fractured parliament that has bedeviled the final years of Macron's presidency, during which France has had five prime ministers in two years.

What is new is the extent to which France is being reshaped by forces now familiar across the globe: a crisis of confidence in democracy, conservative billionaires building media empires and financing ideological movements, polarizing social media, foreign interference in elections, and growing voter distrust of supranational institutions, including the European Union.

France, unlike the United States, places strict limits on campaign spending, but money still shapes the broader political ecosystem. Pierre-Édouard Stérin , a self-described "conservative libertarian," has committed substantial resources to organizations seeking to advance right-wing and far-right agendas. The industrialist Vincent Bolloré has assembled a vast media empire that includes CNews, a Fox News-style channel that has become an important platform for the nationalist right.

Whatever the result of the Presidential elections, the outlook is troubling for Europe. A Le Pen or Mélenchon presidency would test European cohesion on everything from Ukraine and relations with Russia to migration, budgets, and the authority of the European Union. But even a more centrist president would likely lack a strong enough coalition to govern effectively, mirroring the current situation in Germany, where Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hobbled by unpopularity and a surge in support for the far-right Alternative for Deutschland.

With France and Germany together accounting for roughly 40% of the E.U. economy, political weakness in both capitals would deprive Europe of its traditional engine at a particularly dangerous moment. Europe faces mounting pressure on three fronts: China's industrial onslaught, reflected in an annual trade deficit of roughly €360 billion; Russia's war against Ukraine and escalating " gray warfare " operations; and the American turn against the postwar international order on which Europe has long depended. All this comes as Europe must also prepare for the profound disruptions of climate change and AI.

The remedy laid out by Mario Draghi, famed for rescuing the euro during his tenure as president of the European Central Bank, calls for greater integration of the single market, more investment and industrial consolidation, and a greater capacity to act collectively. France is indispensable to any such reforms. A politically paralyzed France would leave Europe weaker at precisely the moment when it can least afford it.

At the heart of the French Revolution of 1789 was the abolition of the privileges of the aristocracy and clergy. Close to two and a half centuries later, privilege remains deeply embedded in French society, dispersed across an array of almost caste-like social and professional groups, from journalists, lawyers, and intellectuals to civil servants and unionized workers, each with its own advantages, protections, pension arrangements, and claims on state resources. The result is a politics in which almost everyone agrees that reform is urgently needed, provided someone else pays, and their own group's advantages remain untouched.

If this sounds like an overreading of 1789, consider Macron's own choice of title for the book that launched his presidential bid: Révolution . His presidency may not have proved entirely revolutionary, yet many of his larger prescriptions have aged well: governments around the world have embraced state-led industrial policy, greater strategic autonomy, and reduced dependence on fossil fuels, while distrust of American hegemony and calls for deeper European integration have gained traction as the postwar order fragments.

Macron can also claim some credit for preserving, and in places renewing, France's traditional strengths: an electricity system powered largely by nuclear energy, global leadership in luxury goods, tourism and hospitality, and a deep reservoir of scientific talent, now exemplified by Mistral, Europe's closest thing to a world-class AI contender.

A skilled diplomat and relentless advocate for the multilateral system, Macron has also taken principled stands on Ukraine, Gaza, Lebanon, debt relief for the world's poorest countries, and climate change, while carefully navigating France's relationships with America and China. France's permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council gives it diplomatic weight far beyond the country's economic size, a status French diplomats ironically describe as "flying first class on an economy ticket."

Yet neither these prescriptions nor these assets have been enough to reverse France's decline over the past two decades. Perhaps what has been missing is a revolution not so much in policy as in political culture: a new social compact in which the sacrifices required to adjust to France's reduced means and diminished relative power are accepted because the burdens are seen to be shared fairly. If such a revolution is to come, it is less likely to start in the Élysée or the ministries than among the students in the streets demanding to be heard.

articles.title: Democrats' latest gun-control push runs into inconvenient fact about how school killer was stopped
articles.summary: An armed bystander helped end the deadly Oregon school shooting, but the gun control debate now centers on whether gun-free zones made it worse.
articles.body:
Democrats renewed calls for tougher gun laws after three children and a teacher were killed in an Oregon school shooting, but gun-rights advocates say the circumstances of the attack bolster their case against new restrictions.

The teenage shooter reportedly opened fire with a shotgun purchased by his mother before an armed father-of-two-students, Kaylub Giamanco, pursued him into Silver Rail Elementary School and fatally shot him. Second Amendment advocates argue additional gun restrictions would not have stopped the killer and could make it harder for armed civilians like Giamanco to intervene.

"Democrats are shamefully weaponizing this tragedy in Oregon to advance their political agenda on gun control," Aidan Johnston, director of federal affairs for Gun Owners of America, told Fox News Digital.

"But more gun control isn't the solution. The school was a gun-free zone, and the killer didn't use a so-called 'assault weapon.' What did stop the mass murderer and save lives was an armed bystander with good aim."

Gun-rights researcher John Lott, president of the Crime Prevention Research Center (CPRC), separately argued that restrictions on carrying guns can leave potential victims defenseless.

"These gun-free zones actually serve as a magnet for these attacks rather than stopping them from occurring," Lott told Fox News Digital.

Lott pointed to CPRC research examining active shootings from 2014 through 2024, which he said found that legally armed civilians stopped more attacks than police did.

The National Rifle Association similarly questioned whether new restrictions would have changed the outcome.

"Oregon already has nearly every gun-control measure on the anti-gun wish list — including an A- rating from groups that push them — yet that did not prevent this attack," the NRA said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"The armed bystander who pursued the shooter inside and ended the threat is the clearest reminder that, when seconds count, a prepared law-abiding citizen can stop a killer."

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., was among the lawmakers calling for action after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where Bend-LaPine school policy bans firearms, including concealed guns.

"The best way to honor these victims is to at long last pass commonsense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools," Wyden said in a statement.

Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., whose district includes Bend, also called for action while acknowledging the armed bystander's intervention.

"When are we going to practice that same bravery that that bystander had?" Bynum asked during a vigil, after urging action to keep guns away from people who should not have them.

Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Jack Reed, D-R.I., also cited the shooting in calling for additional gun laws and urging the Supreme Court to change course.

"It is far past time for the Roberts Court to make it clear their decision on guns does not endorse unfettered and unregulated access to weapons," Reed said.

"In the absence of the Supreme Court ceasing its pro-gun rulings, Republicans need to join Democrats in enacting commonsense policies that could prevent these kinds of tragedies."

The Roberts court has issued consequential gun-rights rulings, including District of Columbia v. Heller, which struck down the District of Columbia's handgun ban in 2008, and New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn. v. Bruen, which struck down New York's requirement that applicants show a special need to obtain a license to carry a handgun in public.

The political fighting is unfolding as investigators examine how the teenage gunman gained access to his mother's shotgun, a key question in determining whether existing or proposed gun laws could have made a difference.

Asked specifically about universal background checks and red-flag laws , the NRA argued that neither would likely have prevented the shooting, citing initial reports that the teenager obtained a family member's firearm.

The organization noted that background checks generally apply to firearm transfers, not unauthorized access to a firearm already owned by someone else. It also argued that a red-flag order would likely have been ineffective, although the circumstances surrounding the teenager's access to the shotgun remain unclear.

Lott also pointed to a 2021 change in Oregon law that allowed individual school districts to prohibit concealed carry permit holders from bringing guns onto school property, arguing that such restrictions can leave schools more vulnerable.

Before that change, Lott said, Oregon teachers with concealed carry permits generally could carry guns at schools, although some districts imposed employment-related restrictions. He estimated that roughly 25 of the state's 197 school districts have adopted prohibitions since then.

"All the school shootings where anybody has been wounded or killed have occurred in places where people, teachers and staff are banned from having guns," Lott said, citing CPRC research.

Lott said his organization is updating the research through 2025. He also argued that uniformed school resource officers face tactical disadvantages because attackers can identify them, avoid them or target them first.

"Having somebody in uniform is like having a neon sign above them that says, shoot me first," Lott said.

Lott also questioned whether penalties for violating gun-free zone restrictions would deter someone already facing multiple life sentences for murder.

"They may be facing six or seven life sentences [on murder counts and the like]. Does taking five years away from their seventh or eighth life [sentence] going to matter? Is that a penalty for them? And the answer is no," he said.

The NRA also cited research finding that 94% of mass shootings since 1950 occurred in gun-free zones, echoing Lott's argument.

"Law-abiding Americans have the right to defend themselves and their communities rather than rely solely on a sign or sticker. The tragedy in Bend is a clear example of how an armed citizen who is prepared and willing to act can stop an attacker and save lives. Policies that keep responsible people disarmed near schools leave those locations more vulnerable, not safer," an NRA spokesperson said.

Lott maintained that gun-free zone restrictions can therefore disadvantage lawful gun owners without meaningfully deterring someone planning a mass shooting.

Fox News Digital's James Cirrone and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: FEMA lays groundwork to shift disaster burden to states
articles.summary: The Trump administration wants states to build their own disaster capacity, and is also considering moving FEMA workers out of Washington, D.C.
articles.body:
The Trump administration plans to reduce state and local dependency on federal disaster aid and could move Federal Emergency Management Agency workers out of Washington, D.C., according to an internal FEMA memo obtained by POLITICO.

FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton wrote in an Oct. 15 memo — confirmed by two people with direct knowledge of it — that the agency will "strengthen state and local emergency management capacity" in an effort to lower reliance on the federal government.

"Reducing federal dependency requires partners to build, maintain, and exercise the capabilities needed to manage incidents effectively," the seven-page memo to agency employees says.

In a separate section, the memo says, "FEMA must reduce unnecessary centralization in Washington, D.C.," and that "regional and field teams are often closest to disaster survivors, state and local officials, emergency managers, and community partners."

The memo is the clearest indication that the administration will follow through on President Donald Trump's long-stated desire to shift disaster management to states and reduce the federal role in preparation and recovery.

It's also the first indication of Hamilton's priorities since he became the first permanent FEMA administrator in Trump's second term in August. A series of acting leaders had run FEMA since January 2025, and their temporary status precluded the agency from making structural changes.

Although Trump has called for weakening FEMA since his first week in office, no new policies emerged, creating uncertainty about the future of federal disaster aid.

Trump has indirectly discouraged reliance on federal disaster aid by taking far longer than his predecessors — including Trump in his first term — to act on state requests for help after major storms, floods, wildfires and other disasters.

Hamilton's memo echoes recommendations of a Trump-appointed FEMA review panel to build state and local capacity and make it harder for states to qualify for federal disaster aid.

The memo also has general language about "eliminating unnecessary steps, reducing administrative burden" and taking other action to expedite and simplify FEMA's notoriously slow and laborious process of approving aid.

Shana Udvardy of the Union of Concerned Scientists said she worries that the memo "seems to promote efficiency and accountability over the welfare of communities."

"When you have a lot of focus on accountability and efficiency, you're going to have staff losing focus on the bigger picture of resiliency," said Udvardy, UCS' senior climate policy resilience analyst. "It's really hard to know what this is going to look like in practice."

FEMA did not respond to a request for comment on the memo.

The agency has limited ability to revise its own policies, which are mostly set by federal law. Congress hasn't changed FEMA operations significantly since 2018, and congressional leaders have shown little interest in bipartisan legislation to overhaul the agency.

Hamilton says in his memo that the objectives he outlined "will guide FEMA's planning, budgeting, program management, operations, and partner engagement. Each office, region, and program must assess whether its current activities align with these priorities and identify opportunities to improve execution."

articles.title: Santuário de Aparecida: movimento segue intenso após 12 de outubro | G1
articles.standfirst: Basílica recebeu peregrinos neste sábado (17), que aproveitaram o fim de semana para agradecer por graças alcançadas e cumprir promessas após as celebrações do Dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.
articles.summary: O Santuário de Aparecida registrou grande fluxo de peregrinos neste sábado (17) para agradecer por graças e cumprir promessas após o Dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.
articles.body:
O primeiro sábado após o feriado de 12 de outubro foi de grande movimentação no Santuário Nacional de Aparecida , no interior de São Paulo. Neste sábado (17), devotos de diferentes regiões do país visitaram a Basílica para rezar diante da imagem de Nossa Senhora Aparecida , agradecer por bênçãos recebidas e cumprir promessas.

Mesmo após as celebrações do Dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, a movimentação continuou no santuário. Muitos peregrinos escolheram o fim de semana seguinte à data para fazer a visita e vivenciar momentos de fé.

Famílias viajaram de diferentes partes do Brasil para visitar a Casa da Mãe Aparecida, com relatos de devoção, agradecimento e pagamento de promessas.

No dia 12 de outubro, quando foi celebrado o Dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, o Santuário Nacional recebeu mais de 200 mil pessoas, segundo os dados informados para as celebrações deste ano.

A data também foi marcada pela presença de cerca de 52 mil romeiros que percorreram a pé trechos da Rodovia Presidente Dutra (BR-116) em direção à basílica.

articles.title: Gado é encontrado morto com suspeita de ter sido atingido por raio  | G1
articles.standfirst: Ao todo, oito bois jovens da raça Nelore foram encontrados mortos em Flórida Paulista (SP). Valor do prejuízo foi estimado em R$ 45 mil.
articles.summary: As cabeças de gado de um proprietário rural de Flórida Paulista (SP) foram encontradas mortas após as fortes chuvas que atingiram a região na última semana.
articles.body:
Oito bois foram encontrados mortos no bairro Mandaguari, na zona rural de Flórida Paulista (SP), após as fortes chuvas que atingiram a região de Presidente Prudente .

A suspeita do proprietário, Bruno Cesar, é de que um raio tenha atingido os animais durante o temporal. Os bois foram encontrados mortos próximos uns dos outros.

Ao g1 , Bruno disse que soube da situação no início da tarde de quarta-feira (14), após um vizinho ter visto os animais mortos e tê-lo avisado. A princípio, apenas a propriedade dele foi afetada.

“Tem uns 25 anos que crio [gado] e essa é a primeira vez. Foi uma perda significante, mas poderia ter sido pior.”

Ao todo, oito garrotes com idade aproximada de dois anos morreram, segundo Bruno. No caso, garrote é o termo utilizado para a fase em que os bois são considerados jovens.

Os animais eram da raça Nelore, considerada uma das mais criadas no Brasil. Eles eram criados por Bruno para revenda posteriormente. O prejuízo estimado pelo produtor é de R$ 45 mil.

articles.title: Maria do Carmo propõe BRT e via expressa para Manaus em caminhada | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidata ao governo do Amazonas pelo PL conversou com eleitores e lojistas e falou sobre BRT, via expressa e pavimentação de ruas no interior.
articles.summary: Maria do Carmo, candidata ao governo do Amazonas, defende a criação de um BRT, uma nova via expressa em Manaus e a pavimentação de ruas no interior do estado.
articles.body:
Maria do Carmo faz caminhada no Centro de Manaus e apresenta propostas para infraestrutura. — Foto: Reprodução/Rede Amazônica

A candidata ao governo do Amazonas, Professora Maria do Carmo (PL), fez uma caminhada pela Avenida Eduardo Ribeiro, no Centro de Manaus , neste sábado (17). Ao lado de apoiadores, ela percorreu ruas da região comercial, cumprimentou eleitores e conversou com lojistas.

Durante a agenda de campanha, Maria do Carmo apresentou propostas para a infraestrutura do estado. Na capital, ela defendeu a implantação de um sistema de transporte rápido por ônibus (BRT) e a construção de uma via expressa para ligar as zonas Oeste e Sul de Manaus. Para o interior, a candidata apontou a pavimentação de ruas como prioridade.

A candidata afirmou que a via expressa planejada deve facilitar o deslocamento entre a região da Ponta Negra e o bairro de Aparecida.

“Na nossa capital, a gente tem aí o planejamento da quarta via, que seria a Via Expressa Oeste, que vai ligar de forma mais rápida, desde a Ponta Negra até Aparecida. Aqui é a nossa cidade, para desafogar o trânsito, a gente vai fazer o BRT também”, declarou.

Maria do Carmo também disse que pretende melhorar as entradas de Manaus para receber quem chega à capital.

“Agora, no interior, é a pavimentação de ruas”, afirmou.

articles.title: Doações de Elon Musk para beneficiar partido de Trump reacendem debate sobre financiamento de campanha | G1
articles.standfirst: Desde o ano passado, o empresário já doou US$ 366 milhões para organizações ligadas ao partido do presidente dos EUA.
articles.summary: Desde o ano passado, o empresário já doou US$ 366 milhões para organizações ligadas ao partido do presidente dos EUA.
articles.body:
As doações do trilionário Elon Musk para beneficiar o partido de Donald Trump , reacenderam o debate sobre o financiamento da campanha. Daqui a menos de três semanas, os americanos vão às urnas eleger um novo Congresso.

Ele doou US$ 360 milhões desde 2025 – o equivalente a mais de R$ 1,8 bilhões.

As doações marcam uma mudança no comportamento do empresário mais rico do mundo.

Depois de trabalhar no recém-criado Departamento de Eficiência Interna no início do governo Trump, o trilionário rompeu publicamente com o presidente. Os dois chegaram a trocar insultos nas redes sociais.

Mas as desavenças não duraram muito. Na semana passada, Trump deu a Musk a maior honraria científica dos Estados Unidos. E o trilionário se tornou uma espécie de consultor do Pentágono para tecnologias militares do futuro.

Desde 2025, deputados do Partido Democrata, de oposição, têm pressionado por investigações contra Musk por conflitos de interesses na época em que trabalhou para o governo.

A acusação é de que ele obteve vantagens em contratos bilionários assinados entre a Space-X e a Nasa. E obteve incentivos do governo para suas empresas.

As leis de financiamento de campanha mudaram muito nos Estados Unidos nas últimas duas décadas. E são bem diferentes das brasileiras.

No Brasil, o financiamento é quase todo público, doações de pessoas são limitadas e de empresas são proibidas.

Já nos EUA, quase todo o recurso é de origem privada. Há limites para doações diretas para candidatos ou partidos.

Mas hoje, os grandes doadores e até empresas podem destinar somas ilimitadas para uma espécie de comitê político. São os chamados Super-PACs.

Eles são um elemento fundamental no jogo financeiro da política americana. São organizações privadas independentes, não ligadas diretamente aos candidatos, e que podem gastar o quanto quiserem em propagandas a favor de uma pessoa ou atacando adversários, desde que não doem o dinheiro diretamente para a campanha.

Musk é dono de um Super PAC. E também fez doações milionárias para outros como o dele.

É um modelo muito criticado por especialistas como Michael Kang Kank, da Universidade de Chicago, e o analista político Brian Rosenwald.

Kank afirma que, com regras pouco rígidas, os mais ricos passam a influenciar ainda mais as eleições. E que, historicamente, os dois partidos se aproveitam disso e, depois, tem uma preocupação em especial em “satisfazer” seus doadores.

Brian Rosenwald diz que Musk não necessariamente está em busca de troca de favores, mas quer financiar um governo alinhado com as suas posições.

O analista político afirma que o modelo deixa as eleições ainda mais caras, com gastos ilimitados. E que nada disso é bom para a democracia.

articles.title: Depois de Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro diz ser prejudicado pela Meta e pede para TSE proibir impulsionamento de posts negativos | G1
articles.standfirst: Advogados do candidato do PL pediram para ingressar na ação já ajuizada por Lula contra a big tech. Flávio aponta que empresa é 'negligente' com propaganda negativa e que está 'enxugando gelo'
articles.summary: Advogados do candidato do PL pediram para ingressar na ação já ajuizada por Lula contra a big tech. Flávio aponta que empresa é 'negligente' com propaganda negativa e que está 'enxugando gelo'
articles.body:
A campanha do candidato a presidente Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) acionou o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) nesta sexta (16) sustentando que tem sido prejudicada pela Meta, big tech responsável por Facebook, Instagram e WhatsApp.

Segundo a campanha, "no segundo turno, é a candidatura de Flávio que vem sofrendo, em escala muito superior, com a distribuição paga de propaganda negativa" , apesar de a legislação proibir impulsionamento de conteúdo negativo nas redes sociais.

Para os advogados de Flávio, a Meta não vem cumprindo seu dever de evitar a propaganda negativa paga .

"A negligência da Meta está a converter a vida da campanha de Flávio e do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral num eterno e inaceitável enxugar de gelo", afirmam os advogados.

Flavio Bolsonaro cumpre agenda na Região dos Lagos e Norte Fluminense — Foto: Ludmila Lopes

A campanha do candidato do PL acionou o TSE no mesmo processo ajuizado na última quarta-feira (14) pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) contra a Meta . Flávio pediu ao TSE para ingressar naquele processo, que já teve decisão favorável a Lula , na condição de terceiro interessado.

Os advogados de Flávio afirmam que está havendo "um derrame de conteúdo negativo ilicitamente impulsionado pela página oficial de Lula", além de um "derrame de mais conteúdo negativo por impulsionamentos ilegais feitos por páginas fantasmas, pessoas físicas (que não podem impulsionar) e pessoas jurídicas (sindicatos e blogs de esquerda, por exemplo)".

A equipe da campanha apresenta no documento ao TSE vários levantamentos numéricos e exemplos de posts que considera irregulares e que tiveram grande alcance.

Ao final, os advogados de Flávio pedem, entre outras medidas, que:

seja determinado à Meta que, até o término do segundo turno, impeça as pessoas físicas e jurídicas que não são candidatos, partidos, federações ou coligações de contratar impulsionamento, porque a lei não autoriza contratações por terceiros;

seja determinado à Meta que impeça, inclusive aos candidatos e partidos, impulsionamento pago de conteúdo com fatos "notoriamente inverídicos" ou "gravemente descontextualizados";

seja determinado à Meta que "se abstenha de aprovar e de entregar impulsionamento de propaganda negativa contra qualquer das candidaturas que disputam o segundo turno", suspendendo, em 24 horas, os anúncios desse tipo que estiverem sendo veiculados.

Os pedidos serão analisados pelo ministro do TSE Marco Aurélio Bellizze .

Nesta sexta (16), após o TSE determinar que a Meta não interfira na distribuição de conteúdo político-eleitoral nem de Lula, nem de Flávio, a empresa afirmou que "não toma partido nessa nem em nenhuma outra eleição" .

"Nossos sistemas não classificam nem distribuem conteúdo com base em ideologia política, e nossas regras e sua aplicação valem igualmente para todos", declarou em nota .

articles.title: Lobista diz que Lulinha se reunia com ministros e afirma querer fazer delação premiada | G1
articles.standfirst: Em entrevista à CNN Brasil, Roberta Luchsinger, investigada sob suspeita de tráfico de influência junto com Lulinha, filho do presidente, afirmou que vem sofrendo ameaças desde que o mandatário a criticou publicamente.
articles.summary: Em entrevista à CNN Brasil, Roberta Luchsinger, investigada sob suspeita de tráfico de influência junto com Lulinha, filho do presidente, afirmou que vem sofrendo ameaças desde que o mandatário a criticou publicamente.
articles.body:
A empresária e lobista Roberta Luchsinger rebateu neste sábado (17) as declarações do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva de que ela seria uma "pilantra". Ela afirmou que, desde que Lula a criticou, vem sofrendo ameaças.

Roberta é amiga de Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, o Lulinha, filho do presidente. Ela e Lulinha são investigados em três inquéritos no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) que apuram se os dois cometeram tráfico de influência em órgãos do governo federal para beneficiar empresários.

"Durante todo esse processo [das investigações] eu venho sendo imensamente agredida. No momento que o presidente da República foi ao ar para mais de 200 milhões de telespectadores, falar que eu era uma pilantra por uma, duas, três vezes, eu tive que tomar a minha própria defesa, porque eu venho sendo constantemente ameaçada de morte", disse Roberta em entrevista à CNN Brasil.

Roberta Luchsinger em entrevista à CNN Brasil — Foto: Reprodução/CNN Brasil

"As minhas filhas sofrem ameaça, as minhas filhas [vêm] sofrendo bullying, porque, a partir do momento que um presidente da República marca na minha testa que eu sou uma pilantra, ele dá um apito para todo esse tipo de agressão", afirmou Roberta.

"Eu não sou pilantra. Eu sou uma mulher sozinha com duas filhas que está enfrentando um processo que eu tenho certeza que 1% não aguentaria o que eu estou passando com duas filhas", disse.

Em agosto, em entrevista à TV Globo , o presidente foi questionado sobre as suspeitas contra Lulinha, reveladas após a apreensão do celular de Roberta pela Polícia Federal , e respondeu: "O que uma pilantra pode fazer num telefone ou o que um cara qualquer pode fazer num telefone?".

Para Roberta, com essa declaração, Lula a colocou como "um boi de piranha, fazendo um 'X' na minha testa". Ela criticou a diferença de tratamento que o presidente deu para ela e para o filho Lulinha.

À CNN Brasil, a equipe de comunicação de Lula afirmou que o presidente "desconhece inteiramente os fatos relatados pela senhora Roberta Luchsinger". A nota diz ainda que o petista jamais manteve qualquer interlocução com a lobista e nunca recebeu demandas dela.

O g1 entrou em contato com o Palácio do Planalto, mas não recebeu retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Questionada pelos jornalistas, Roberta também falou sobre a relação de Lulinha com integrantes do governo. Em uma declaração de Lula ao podcast Flow, em 1º de outubro, o presidente foi questionado sobre as suspeitas contra seu filho e disse que duvidava que Lulinha tivesse tratado de contratos e negócios com ministros.

"Eu duvido que meu filho tenha feito lobby com qualquer ministro meu. Duvido que meu filho tenha conversado com alguém a respeito disso [contratos públicos]", disse Lula ao Flow.

Já Roberta disse neste sábado que presenciou Lulinha sentado conversando com ministros "inúmeras vezes", mas não especificou quais os assuntos tratados nessas conversas. "Inclusive [Lulinha] viajou para a casa do ministro Camilo [Santana], no Ceará", exemplificou.

"O filho dele [Lulinha] sentava semanalmente com ministro, seja para trocar figurinhas, seja para trocar qualquer outro tipo de diálogo", declarou Roberta.

Em nota, o senador Camilo Santana afirma que nunca esteve com Lulinha para tratar de qualquer assunto de governo ou de qualquer tipo de negócio. O comunicado diz ainda que o senador não tem relação alguma com Roberta.

Os jornalistas perguntaram se Roberta presenciou Lulinha conversando com algum ministro sobre a venda de canabidiol ao Ministério da Saúde, um dos temas investigados pela Polícia Federal em um dos inquéritos no STF. Roberta respondeu que, na presença dela, não.

Em outro trecho da entrevista, Roberta disse que pode fechar acordo de delação premiada com as autoridades, sem poupar ninguém, embora entenda que não cometeu crime algum.

Para um acordo de delação ser assinado, é preciso que o colaborador confesse que praticou crimes e entregue provas que ajudem a polícia a esclarecer o caso.

A lobista disse que poderia colaborar apresentando "talvez detalhes que não estão ali dentro do WhatsApp, porque a vida da gente não é só no WhatsApp".

"Eu estarei lá pronta para colaborar. Eu quero fazer uma delação premiada. Sabe por quê? Porque eu não tenho pai presidente. Eu não tenho mãe presidente. Eu sou uma mulher com duas filhas", disse Roberta.

articles.title: STJ abre investigação e exonera servidor suspeito de vazar minutas de decisões a advogado amigo de Flávio | G1
articles.standfirst: As trocas de mensagens constam em um relatório da Polícia Federal encaminhado à Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR).
articles.summary: As trocas de mensagens constam em um relatório da Polícia Federal encaminhado à Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR).
articles.body:
Fachada do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) — Foto: TV Gazeta

O Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) abriu uma investigação e exonerou, nesta sexta-feira (16), um servidor da área de tecnologia suspeito de vazar minutas de decisões do tribunal ao advogado Willer Tomaz , amigo do senador e candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL)

As trocas de mensagens constam em um relatório da Polícia Federal (PF) encaminhado à Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR).

De acordo com o relatório, em uma delas, Humberto Fontoura Pradera, então servidor da área de tecnologia do STJ, repassou ao advogado Willer Tomaz informações relacionadas a demandas internas do tribunal. Ele contou que duas pessoas haviam sido designadas para tratar de determinado assunto e afirmou que manteria o advogado informado.

Outro episódio aponta que Pradera encaminhou uma fotografia de um documento exibido na tela de um computador, com um carimbo sobre a mesa.

"O presidente do STJ, ministro Luis Felipe Salomão, tomou conhecimento dos fatos, e um procedimento interno para apuração já havia sido instaurado desde a semana passada. Como não se trata de concursado, o servidor em cargo de confiança foi exonerado nesta sexta-feira (16)", afirmou o STJ, em nota. O caso foi revelado pelo portal UOL e confirmado pela TV Globo .

"As medidas criminais estão em andamento e são sigilosas, e sobre elas o Tribunal não vai se manifestar", informou o STJ.

Pradera ocupava uma posição de destaque no tribunal exercendo o cargo de secretário de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (STI). Antes disso, também havia sido assessor-chefe da Assessoria de Inteligência Artificial do STJ, participando de projetos ligados à transformação digital, à inteligência artificial e aos sistemas internos do tribunal.

Em outra troca de mensagens que consta no documento, ao ser questionado por Willer sobre “qual o número deles?”, Pradera respondeu que “essa tá no REsp 2122969” e afirmou que a tutela teria perdido efeito em razão do julgamento. Segundo os investigadores, a conversa mostra o compartilhamento de informações sobre o processo, acompanhado de explicações sobre seus possíveis efeitos.

Além de Pradera, o advogado mantinha conversas com o subprocurador-geral da República Antônio Carlos Simões Martins Soares (ele se aposentou de forma voluntária em março de 2026).

O relatório mostra uma planilha em que a PF compara o teor dos pareceres com o que é recomendado por Willer ao subprocurador. Em alguns casos, os trechos são idênticos, em outros a redação é semelhante à sugerida pelo advogado.

Segundo a PF, em mais de uma vez o posicionamento de Antônio Carlos seguiu as recomendações do advogado na elaboração de seus pareceres.

O documento ilustra o caso de um agravo em recurso especial no qual parte da mensagem encaminhada por Willer aparece posteriormente reproduzidas de forma literal ou praticamente literal em um parecer, com referências ao desconto de quase 90%, ao valor do FII Eldorado, à exclusão de créditos considerados ruins, aos laudos sigilosos e à atuação do administrador judicial.

O relatório traz outro caso de uma discussão prévia sobre tese relacionada à gestão de conta do espólio; posteriormente, Antônio Carlos Martins Soares opinou pelo provimento.

O advogado Willer Tomaz, um dos donos do jato em que o senador e candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) viajou, em janeiro do ano passado , é investigado pela PF na Operação Sem Desconto, que investiga um esquema bilionário de fraudes em benefícios do INSS.

Em outra apuração, a PF investiga suposta lavagem de dinheiro por meio de jogos em uma casa de apostas . Ao todo, em 18 meses (de janeiro de 2025 a julho de 2026), Tomaz apostou R$ 6,6 bilhões e teve um prejuízo de R$ 188,5 milhões.

Os dados foram informados pela defesa do advogado em um processo aberto contra a casa de apostas Blaze, que patrocina o atacante do Santos, Neymar Jr, e que tinha contrato com a influenciadora, Virgínia Fonseca.

Nesta sexta-feira (16), a Justiça de São Paulo negou um pedido de Tomaz de devolução de R$ 163 milhões perdidos em bets. O advogado acionou a 44ª Vara Cível de São Paulo para tentar reaver a quantia que diz ter perdido em apostas online na Blaze, alegando vício em jogos e falhas da plataforma.

Relatório da PF também mostra que Flávio Bolsonaro foi cadastrado como "usuário master" de uma conta bancária pertencente a uma empresa do advogado . Para a PF, o cadastro dava a Flávio "acesso operacional relevante" à conta bancária e "sustenta a hipótese de sua eventual participação econômica ou societária de fato na empresa".

O advogado afirmou que não teve acesso indevido a documentos e não interferiu em manifestações do Ministério Público Federal. Veja a nota na íntegra:

"O advogado Willer Tomaz nega categoricamente ter tido acesso irregular ou não autorizado a decisões judiciais ou a pareceres do Ministério Público Federal, bem como ter interferido em qualquer manifestação. As insinuações são falsas, configuram desinformação e revelam desconhecimento elementar, ou deliberada distorção, do funcionamento dos tribunais.

A ciência antecipada de julgados no Superior Tribunal de Justiça não é crime: é funcionalidade prevista no próprio sistema da Corte. Tampouco há ilícito quando um procurador, convencido pelos memoriais apresentados, incorpora seus argumentos ao parecer. Isso é contraditório, e converter rotina processual em suspeita é criminalizar a advocacia.

A defesa desconhece o relatório citado e repudia sua divulgação seletiva, em plena campanha eleitoral, com menções a terceiros alheios aos fatos investigados. Ilegal, este sim, é o vazamento de material sigiloso, cujos autores serão identificados e responsabilizados."

A reportagem não localizou os demais citados pela PF.

articles.summary: Um homem de 38 anos foi preso temporariamente, suspeito de envolvimento em uma dupla tentativa de homicídio em uma conveniência de Presidente Prudente (SP), nesta sexta-feira (16).

Homem é preso por suspeita de dupla tentativa de homicídio em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Câmera de Segurança/Polícia Civil

Um homem de 38 anos foi preso temporariamente, suspeito de envolvimento em uma dupla tentativa de homicídio em uma conveniência de Presidente Prudente (SP), nesta sexta-feira (16).

O crime ocorreu na noite da última segunda-feira (12), quando dois homens foram atingidos por disparos de arma de fogo.

Segundo a Polícia Civil, o investigado é apontado como autor dos tiros contra as duas vítimas, que sobreviveram e foram encaminhadas para atendimento médico.

A prisão foi realizada pela 3ª Delegacia de Investigação de Homicídios da Deic/Deinter 8, durante o cumprimento de mandados de prisão temporária e de busca e apreensão.

articles.title: A sleeper Senate battleground has turned into a real Republican liability
articles.summary: The newest addition to the Senate map is giving Republicans headaches.
articles.body:
WICHITA, Kansas — Roger Marshall was running behind.

The bus Kansas Republicans booked for a five-day barnstorming tour sat idling Tuesday morning, with other statewide candidates onboard. The tour was already a few minutes delayed as state party chair Danedri Herbert awaited word from the senator who some Republicans grumble isn't campaigning hard enough as polls show him tied or trailing .

Finally, she got word: Marshall would ride separately.

As the bus reached its first stop in rural Newton, Marshall crept aboard — and was spotted by reporters doing so. He then joined the other candidates exiting to greet the crowd like he'd been there the whole time.

Marshall is playing catch-up as he races to avoid becoming the first person to lose a Senate contest to a Democrat in the state in nearly a century. He faces the most serious challenger for a Kansas senator in over a decade as his party stares down a grim environment under President Donald Trump's second term.

National Republicans are pouring millions into the state to prop him up; national Democrats are responding in kind, and Democrat Adam Hamilton, a well-known United Methodist pastor, is suddenly flush with cash for the campaign's homestretch.

But some Republicans think it's already too late for Marshall.

"He took it way too much for granted," said former Kansas Gov. Mike Hayden, a Republican who supported Marshall's previous campaigns but is now publicly backing Hamilton. "He's been almost invisible, except on national television. And there's not a lot of love in Kansas for Washington D.C."

National Republicans have privately urged Marshall to take his race more seriously on numerous occasions, according to a person familiar with the conversations who was granted anonymity to discuss them. Marshall, this person said, never appeared too worried about the race. Marshall's latest Federal Election Commission report indicates this may be true. He raised just $866,000 for the third quarter to $9.9 million for Hamilton, and that filing did not appear to include any full-time payments to campaign staff.

Marshall's team did not respond to requests for comment on this article.

One Republican strategist close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak candidly, acknowledged the race is an "uphill battle," comparing Marshall to an "old athlete who, it takes them a lot longer to warm up to get ready for the game time, and they didn't start that early enough."

That strategist said that the remaining undecided voters are overwhelmingly Trump voters, and predicted they'd come home. Kansans "are mad at Republicans, but they just hate Democrats more," the strategist said. "As much as DC Republicans are bedwetting, the ones actually working on the races are cognizant of this."

As the race nears the homestretch, a deluge of bad press has dogged the senator: His campaign used pictures of a Kansas campground without permission and had to edit the ad; his team faces accusations of blurring the line between his official and campaign offices; his campaign reportedly didn't pay a bill to a local bakery for six years until after the unpaid debt was made public ( he apologized ).

The first focuses on a Florida property that he owns, raising questions about how much time he actually spends in Kansas. The second stems from a New York Times report that Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist who served two terms in the U.S. House, had allegedly taken legal action against hundreds of medical patients who didn't pay their bills. Marshall has said he spends the bulk of his time in Washington or Kansas, calling the claims "bologna." He called the Times' report a "hit job by left media" and told Fox News he had "nothing else to do to with the process" after patients' accounts went to collections.

At a Monday rally in the liberal college town of Lawrence, Hamilton told supporters that Kansans deserve a senator who isn't just "showing up for photo ops" between "time with your family in Florida."

"I want to know from Roger Marshall: What's your plan when people … show up and they don't have health insurance?" Hamilton said, standing on a hay bale in a shady park. "Is the plan we're going to sue them? Then we're going to have some of them arrested, and maybe a few of them put in jail?"

Hamilton's campaign cut a face-to-camera ad with one of Marshall's former patients, who said she was arrested when she was eight months pregnant because she missed a $50 payment to Marshall's office. The Marshall campaign sent a cease-and-desist letter in response, saying the ad's "message is false in every material respect," and went up this week with its own ad of a former patient singing his praises.

National Republicans have swooped in to prop up Marshall with $11 million in planned spending in recent days. And he's getting other reinforcements: Chris Grant, the stalwart Trump-world operative and veteran of previous Marshall campaigns, will take an expanded role on the senator's team through Election Day, Axios first reported .

Marshall's struggles are drawing unfavorable comparisons to the last Republican who needed to be bailed out to win a Senate race in the state.

"This race reminds me of Sen. Pat Roberts' last race [in 2014], when he was accused of not maintaining a Kansas residence and campaigning poorly," said one Kansas state GOP lawmaker, who was granted anonymity to speak openly.

But Republicans had a strong wind at their backs in 2014, sweeping nearly every Senate race that year; Roberts managed a 10-point win, similar to Marshall's 11-point win in 2020. This time around, the national climate is blowing hard the other direction.

Kansas has been especially hard-hit by some of Trump's policies. His tariffs and spiking fuel prices left the state's row crop farmers struggling. A plan to import cheap foreign beef infuriated ranchers in a state that produces the second-most cattle annually. And his threats to cut off U.S. sales of Bombardier planes — a Canadian company whose U.S. headquarters are in Wichita — rattled the state's robust aviation industry.

Marshall has recently shown signs he knows he's in a fight. The normally strident MAGA backer broke with the president on the beef import plan and on a recent local immigration enforcement action, after ICE activity rattled some of his state's agricultural towns.

He's banking on the conservative nature of the state, working hard to paint Hamilton as a progressive who will fall in line behind Washington Democrats. "This guy is the most radical liberal Democrat in the history of Kansas to get through a primary," Marshall said in an interview in Garden City. "He is this wolf in sheep's clothing."

At rallies in Newton, Hutchinson, Dodge City and Garden City, he warned that his election could decide which party controls the upper chamber. "If my opponent were elected, it would give Chuck Schumer and AOC control of the Senate," he repeated. Recent Republican ads hit Hamilton as "woke" and "radical," pointing to his past praise of the Black Lives Matter movement.

But as Marshall tagged along with the other GOP candidates for their barnstorming tour, holding mini-rallies across central and western Kansas on Tuesday, he was reminded how deep the anger at Washington runs right now — even in ruby-red Kansas.

In Dodge City, the self-described "cattle capital" of the country, some Republicans in the crowd grumbled about spiking fuel prices. In Newton, protesters screamed through Marshall's speech, calling Republicans "fascists." ("Quiet, Satan!" a disgruntled attendee retorted.) In Garden City, where ICE activity sent shockwaves last month, Marshall got an earful in a private meeting with local lawmakers over their frustration that immigration officers barged into town without coordinating with local law enforcement.

"I think the frustration is still there," state Rep. Jason Goetz, a Republican who represents some of the cities affected by ICE enforcement.

There's a belief among some Kansas Republicans that Marshall has thrown together so poor a campaign that if he wins, it won't be of his own accord — it will be because of Ty Masterson, the Republican state Senate president running for governor who joined him on the bus tour and has polled a few points ahead of Marshall in most surveys.

Rep. Tim Huelskamp, a Kansas Republican who lost a U.S. House primary to Marshall in 2016, said Masterson is "going to pull everybody across the line," a list that "absolutely" includes Marshall.

Patricia Woods, a Hutchinson resident, said at a rally that she is "100% behind Masterson." When asked about Marshall, she said she is "kind of on the fence."

Masterson, when asked about Marshall's race, simply chuckled. "It's more complicated than mine," he said.

Adam Wren and Andrew Howard contributed reporting.

articles.title: Insults, odd obsessions and rambling thoughts: a week in Trump rallies
articles.summary: President has hit red states to drum up Republican support – and his increasingly strange performances are on full display
articles.body:
Montana, Tennessee, Alaska. In the run-up to an election, a Republican president typically wouldn't be campaigning in these traditionally red states.

These aren't normal times, however, and Donald Trump, an unpopular president leading an unpopular party, has held rallies in those states in the last week, seeking to drum up support. But a series of eccentric performances from the president means his behavior has been the focus, rather than any of the candidates he is backing.

Trump, 80, has used his appearances to muse about animals' opposition to the second amendment, to call one Republican candidate "nerdy", and to demonstrate a hitherto unexpressed fascination with "asses" – men's and babies', in particular.

Along the way Trump has repeated his lie that 2020 was a rigged election, claimed, falsely , that he has secured $21tn in foreign investment in the US, and issued dark warnings about Democrats. Let's take a look.

Trump was supposed to be in Syracuse to support Bruce Blakeman, the Republican candidate for New York governor, whom he introduced to the crowd in a confusing way. Trump told the crowd of Blakeman: "I've just known him just for a second. I've known him for a long time, years."

Aside from his entirely contradictory explanation of his relationship with Blakeman, Trump went on to claim that, in New York: "You can no longer say: 'Mother – hi, mom'. It's: 'Hi gestating – hi, gestating. I love you so much, gestating.'" People are still allowed to say mother in New York.

Trump continued by talking about one of the things closest to his heart, spending 15 minutes complaining about how he did not win the Nobel peace prize, despite having "settled eight wars".

"Pakistan and India. I called them up, I said: 'If you guys don't stop killing each other I'm going to charge you 250% in tariffs and we're not going to trade with you. They said no, no, no, you cannot do that. I said, yes, I can," Trump said. India has repeatedly denied that a ceasefire was reached because of any intervention from Trump.

A day later, Trump appeared in Clarksville. There, he adopted a strange method of talking to the audience, saying there was "such love", before adding: "I mean, it's amazing. When you stand up here, it's just like… the love. I could say the stupidest things and you clap: "Oh, I love you so … .'"

Trump continued: "It's true. But we don't say the stupidest things. We say things of common sense. We say things that make sense, and we probably are mostly conservative, but it's not really conservative. It's things of common sense."

Speaking in Ohio, Trump said he had recently learned that Jon Husted, the Republican senator running for re-election in the state, played football at university.

Trump continued: "I don't do this with men very often. I started examining [Husted's] body, because I didn't know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole – and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He's got these, like, claws."

Later, Trump praised Husted, 59, for having a good jawline, before turning his attention to insulting immigrants from Somalia. Trump claimed that those people "come from a part of the world that only knows how to kill each other" and said that in Somalia people were "low IQ" and "don't have pants to wear".

Trump was in Alaska to rally support for Dan Sullivan, the Republican senator. It was revealing that he was there at all: this should be deep red territory. Yet the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, is running neck and neck against Sullivan, something which prompted Trump to call Peltola, a native American former tribal judge, "a whack job".

During a meandering speech, Trump also granted pardons, on stage, to two Alaska auto shop owners, who previously pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act.

"When you give somebody a pardon, they say that means – and I don't know how this works and why it's an expression, but it's well used, that means you're as clean as a newborn baby's ass," Trump said.

He added of that phrase: "I never understood that. Why is that so clean? But they – they – they felt that was the definition of cleanliness."

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

After praising Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, as "young" and "handsome" (Sheikh Tamim is 46), Trump turned his attention the Arizona Republicans he was in Bullhead City to support, including Alex Kolodin, a member of the Arizona house of representatives who is seeking higher office.

"Everybody also needs to get out and vote for Alex Kolodin, a warrior for election integrity, as your next secretary of state," Trump said.

"Alex, good luck. You look good. Central casting, actually. You want a secretary of state to look exactly like that, a little bit nerdy, and that's good."

It was reminiscent of Trump's repeated complaints about Ken Paxton, his handpicked nominee for US Senate in Texas. Trump has repeatedly said he does not like how Paxton talks, dresses, or looks.

During his remarks, Trump also managed to add to questions about his health, insult yet another person he knows, and let the crowd know their life was less important than his.

"I travel with more doctors than any human being. If people get sick in the audience, they don't – they leave them alone," Trump said.

"You know what they call them? Collateral damage. If that person right over there, a friend of mine – he looks like shit, actually, he looks – he looks like he's ready to have a heart attack. If he actually had a heart attack, you know what my doctors would do that follow the president, all presidents?

"They would leave him alone. I'd say please help him. No, sir, we can't leave your side. I said but he's dying of a heart attack. Sir, he's collateral damage. Can you believe it? They got, like, six ambulances and they won't use one for anybody else. Anyway – but let's hope we never have that problem."

Trump made a fairly desperate plea to voters, invoking the long-time Republican fear-mongering that Democrats will ban guns – something which is very much not a position of the Democratic party.

"You know who would love that to happen? Some of the wild animals you have up here that like – that like eating you," Trump said.

"We talked about that with Tim [Sheehy, US senator for Montana] and Steve [Daines, the other US senator for Montana] on the plane. That was my first question, I say: 'When you walk out in the woods here, do you always have a gun, Tim?' He said: 'Actually – actually, yes.' I said: 'What about you, Steve?' He said: 'Yes, we're intelligent people.'

"You know, the animals would be very, very happy to see you without guns. They would gain a lot of weight. And leave the law-abiding Americans defenseless while they set loose the savage criminals into your communities."

Even for a president known for eccentricities, Trump's fascination with backsides, the appearance of his friends, and animals, has raised eyebrows. And with two weeks to go until the midterm elections, there will be more appearances to come.

articles.title: Democrats are threatening US AI supremacy. Republicans should pounce.
articles.summary: Republicans have an opportunity to fight for American technological supremacy while also benefiting many of their constituents.
articles.body:
As Democrats show increasing hostility to the artificial intelligence and energy industries, Republicans have an opportunity to fight for American technological supremacy while also benefiting many of their constituents. The next type of computing will be dependent on geography that naturally advantages rural areas in red America and could revive local economies with mostly conservative residents.

A combination of land prices, grid capacity and the simple physics of heat dissipation provide a huge natural advantage to developing red states. Google signed a massive $4.3 billion deal this month to reopen a nuclear power plant in Iowa and upgrade reactors in several other states, with the tech giant entering into a 20-year power purchasing agreement. Electricity from the ​first of the upgraded plants is expected to be delivered in 2028.

At the same time, new data centers planned to be built by 2028 sit on average 175 kilometers from major cities, versus 46 kilometers for the last generation . In other words, they’re becoming more rural. This naturally favors Republican dominated states, because the center of the AI revolution’s infrastructure increasingly relies on their favorable geography, instead of the physical location of software engineers.

Moreover, companies want to build in red America, where acreage is cheap, electrical transmission infrastructure can be added without multi-year litigation and industrial power prices remain competitive. Locations with a friendly regulatory environment and available land will have a huge advantage to get new investment. It’s the digital equivalent of moving a steel mill closer to its supporting coal mine to reduce transportation costs.

Analyses by the commercial real estate firm JLL found that the vast majority of new data centers under construction will be in states that voted for President Trump in 2024. Two-thirds of proposed U.S. facilities are headed for rural counties, largely in the South, as part of a new great migration of business . The rural economic boom from this will be enormous, and going forward many Republican voters will reap the dividend.

Loudoun County, Virginia, which is currently the largest concentration of data centers in the world, will get $1.3 billion in taxes from data centers and related industries next year. That is roughly 40 percent of the county’s revenue, according to The New York Times. That windfall has funded new schools, recreation centers and road work. It also cut residential property taxes by 30 percent . Local officials claim data centers support 15,000 jobs in the broader economy . After all, before the model can run somebody has to mine, refine and manufacture the materials!

Geography isn’t the only factor of course. Red-state utility commissions and legislatures have compounded these natural advantages by moving faster on permitting and other legal concerns. But favorable natural and regulatory environments cluster in places that voted Republican in the last several election cycles, not in blue America.

A recent study by the Pacific Research Institute found that software engineer-heavy and Democrat-led California illustrated the issue in stark terms. The Golden State has pursued aggressive mandates and regulations aiming for 100 percent green electricity by 2045 , while shuttering the Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant . This has created structural power supply shortfalls that cap the growth of data centers, as these facilities cannot function on unreliable solar and wind alone.

Democratic-led energy policies resulted in higher costs and greater legal risks , and ultimately lost economic opportunities. Despite California’s historic status as a tech hub, these foolish policies function as a de facto veto on a key source of future economic growth, a veto potentially more durable and widespread than an outright prohibition.

Ideological constraints on energy threaten to hand a strategic advantage to foreign competitors such as China who have no qualms about expanding their energy supply or computational power.

And many Democrats aren’t just thwarting progress with regulatory hurdles but are pushing outright bans. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Sen. (I-Vt.) Bernie Sanders proposed another Artificial Intelligence (AI) Data Center Moratorium Act in July, which would impose a “temporary” federal pause on the construction of new AI data centers and the expansion of existing ones. This would effectively cede the likely future of the global economy to their far more pro-technology ideological fellow travelers in China.

America leads the world in AI software, algorithms and frontier model development, giving it a decisive edge in the intellectual software race against China. Yet even left-wing groups like the Brookings Institution admit this advantage is increasingly at risk of being neutralized by blue State energy infrastructure failures driven by restrictive energy policies that prioritize intermittent renewables over reliable power.

A data center can sometimes be built in as little as two years, but the major electrical transmission lines and substations often take up to 15 to construct . This means that a major bottleneck is policy.

Without abundant, affordable and always-available electricity, even the best AI models cannot scale to the massive compute clusters required. Democrats have handed Republicans a political win on a silver platter, if the Republicans are wise enough to push back with a strong pro-growth stance that disproportionately enriches red state economies, while also ensuring U.S. technological dominance.

Andrew Follett conducts research analysis for a nonprofit in the Washington area.
