articles.title: Stephen A. Smith calls dinner with Trump, Bill Maher, Kid Rock ‘shocking’
articles.summary: Commentator Stephen A. Smith said he was shocked President Trump hosted him, left-leaning comedian Bill Maher and conservative country star Kid Rock at the White House earlier this week, adding the gathering lasted more than four hours. “It was shocking. I certainly didn’t expect that amount of time,” Smith told CNN’s Laura Coates Friday night.…
articles.body:
Commentator Stephen A. Smith said he was shocked President Trump hosted him, left-leaning comedian Bill Maher and conservative country star Kid Rock at the White House earlier this week, adding the gathering lasted more than four hours.

“It was shocking. I certainly didn’t expect that amount of time,” Smith told CNN’s Laura Coates Friday night. “I give him all the credit in the world because he didn’t run from any questions. Anything we asked him, he kept coming back at us with the things that he had to say.”

While Kid Rock, whose real name is Robert Richie, told a panel on Fox New’s “Fox & Friends” after the Thursday dinner that he has dined with Trump and Maher once in the past, he did not elaborate on why the trio — with obvious political differences — got invited together to meet in the Oval Office.

Smith, an independent political commentator and ESPN personality, said he accepted the invite to discuss his concerns surrounding funding for Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCU). But he said the conversation drifted to include other topics, like the midterms and the economy.

Kid Rock characterized the gathering similarly during his Fox & Friends appearance, where he said that, despite some disagreement, they all conceded that “socialism and communism have no place to have a foothold in our government.”

The president and his party face serious headwinds ahead of the midterms, with voters disapproving of his administration on several issues, including the economy, which he ran on in 2024. Smith said he pressed Trump on economic concerns and the GOP’s position, to which the president responded he was adamant conditions would improve.

“As it pertains to the economy, no, he says what he always says, and he firmly believes in himself,” Smith said. “Obviously everything gets better. That’s his mentality.”

Smith said he also told Trump polls show he is unpopular at the moment, but the president maintained that Republicans see him favorably.

One other topic Smith said raised to Trump was the Texas Senate race, where the president’s choice in the Republican primary was Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton — who won the party’s nomination. Paxton now narrowly trails his Democratic opponent, James Talarico, in many polls.

“I said to him, the real problem is Ken Paxton. It’s a damn shame that [Paxton] … is sitting around scared to debate,” Smith said. “That is a disgrace to me. He should be unqualified for the job.”

Paxton has not accepted invites from Talarico to debate, even as some of his closest allies say he should do so. Trump reportedly said Smith had “a good point” on Paxton’s refusal to debate, according to the commentator.

Smith said he appreciated the chance to fit face to face with Trump, something he said he had not done in years.

“This is the first time I’ve seen him face to face in over a decade and a half, and I saw it as an opportunity to make my case,” Smith said. “Obviously we’ve known each other for many, many years, even though we’ve never spoken outside of one interview since he became president of the United States.”

Trump spoke to reporters about the dinner outside of the White House Friday, describing the gathering as “great” and that “they had a good time.”

“It was a very informative dinner,” the president added. “Smart people. Stephen A. is great. Bill Maher — I will tell you what. He likes me a lot more than people understand, and I actually like him. It was a good dinner.”

articles.title: California diners are cutting back as costs soar — but restaurant owner reveals one trend that's booming
articles.summary: Happy hour business jumped from roughly 8% to nearly 30% of sales at a San Diego restaurant group as California diners hunt for cheaper meals.
articles.body: Happy hour is becoming the main event for some California diners as the state's high cost of living pushes more customers to seek out discounted meals instead of paying full price for a night out. Chef Alex Carballo of Grand Restaurant Group told Fox News Digital that happy hour once accounted for an estimated 5% to 8% of his business. Now, that figure has climbed to nearly 30%, even as customers cut back on dining out. "My happy hour has increased a lot, so I think people are looking for deals and looking for options," Carballo said. The shift reflects a broader affordability squeeze across California where residents told Fox News Digital that rising costs for housing, groceries and gasoline are forcing them to rethink everyday spending. California has the highest overall price levels in the nation, according to 2024 data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, with prices running roughly 11% above the national average. But affordability pressures extend far beyond the Golden State, as Americans nationwide grapple with elevated costs for housing, groceries and other everyday necessities. NEWSOM UNDER FIRE AS CALIFORNIA GAS TAX HIKE SENDS PUMP PRICES EVEN HIGHER Carballo said customers are visiting his restaurants less frequently, with some scaling back how often they eat out. "They're going out three times a week, where they were coming out to see me four or five [times]. And the people that used to see three times a week, they're only coming out once," he said. What was once a stop for drinks or appetizers before dinner is increasingly becoming the dinner itself, Carballo said. "Now it's like, that's where they're going and they're hitting those scenes," he said. Customers can still enjoy the same food, service and atmosphere at lower prices, Carballo said, making happy-hour deals particularly appealing. But those discounts also create challenges for restaurant operators who are already grappling with rising expenses. "I'm still paying the same amount for food. I'm still paying the employees. My rent didn't change. Nothing changed. Only thing I'm doing is trying to discount my product to gain people to come here," Carballo said. AMERICANS SAY TIPPING PRACTICES 'HAVE BECOME RIDICULOUS' AS DIGITAL PROMPTS PUSH HIGHER GRATUITIES Fox News Digital also spoke with residents in Southern California who described making financial trade-offs that extend well beyond restaurants. Jonas, a Santa Monica resident who is planning a wedding with his fiancée, said he and his fiancée are reevaluating their budget as everyday expenses continue to add up. "Certainly gas is expensive, rent is high, and then grocery prices are pretty high as well," Jonas said. He estimated that he spends approximately $100 a week on groceries and said rising costs are influencing their decisions about dining out and transportation. The couple is "eating out a little bit less," Jonas said, adding that he has also started walking to work to "save money on gas as well." "I think that people are just seeing prices go up everywhere, and feeling like they're getting less than what they had four years ago maybe," he said. "I think everybody's really feeling that." BELOVED RESTAURANT CHAIN DWINDLES FROM 850 LOCATIONS TO 87, BUT EXPERT SEES 'A LOT OF LIFE LEFT' For some Californians, the financial strain has gone beyond cutting back on restaurants. Justin, a California native from Glendora who moved to Las Vegas seven years ago, told Fox News Digital that the state's high cost of living was one of the reasons he left. "Affordability is crazy," Justin said while visiting Los Angeles for a Rams game. "I left seven years ago and I thought gas and you know rent was high then," he said. "Here I am seven years later and it's ... one of the reasons why I'm in Vegas now. It's just unaffordable." Justin said many of his friends who remain in California are still struggling with housing costs. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE LA'S HOMELESS HELLSCAPE — UNLIKELY CRITICS BLAST DEMS AS GOP HOPEFUL TOURS SKID ROW "90% of my friends are living with a roommate. It is really hard to live alone here," he said. Housing remains another major affordability challenge in the Golden State. Just 19% of California households could afford the state's median-priced home of $916,750 in the second quarter of 2026, according to the California Association of Realtors. "Everything is more expensive, gas is more expensive, food," she told Fox News Digital. "There's really very few affordable restaurants left on Abbot Kinney. Even our local co-op prices have gone up at least 15%. Everything costs more." "We're not getting any breaks in California," she said.

articles.title: Joy Behar wants Trump back on ‘The View’ despite saying he’s ‘not long for this world’
articles.summary: Joy Behar invited Trump back to "The View" while claiming he's "not long for this world," prompting a sharp response from the White House team.
articles.body: "The View" co-host Joy Behar extended an unlikely invitation Friday to her longtime political foe President Donald Trump, saying she would welcome him back to the daytime talk show despite suggesting that he is "not long for this world." Behar, who has said she wants her legacy to include helping remove Trump from office, reflected on her decades-long history with the president during an interview with New York Magazine. "I’d love Donald Trump to take the heat," said the longtime Trump critic. "You know Trump is not long for this world. He seems ill. He does not seem like he’s well," Behar added. BILL MAHER REVEALS HE'S HAVING DINNER WITH TRUMP AGAIN, SAYS HE WAS 'REALLY NICE' BY TEXT A White House spokesperson responded to Behar’s comments about Trump’s well-being in a statement to Fox News Digital. "‘Joyless’ Behar is an extremely unlikeable, talentless hack with a poorly rated TV show who clearly suffers from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome," the statement said. "I lose braincells every single time I have the displeasure of hearing her speak," the spokesperson continued. TRUMP DECLARED 'FULLY FIT' FOR ALL PRESIDENTIAL DUTIES AFTER ANNUAL PHYSICAL SHOWS 'EXCELLENT HEALTH' Behar’s comments mark the latest instance in which "The View" co-host has publicly questioned Trump’s health. Last month, she argued that the media does not scrutinize Trump’s health to the same degree it scrutinized former President Joe Biden’s. Despite their bitter political divide today, Behar and Trump share a history from long before his political career. Trump made more than a dozen appearances on "The View" before he was president and Behar even attended his wedding to Marla Maples at The Plaza Hotel in 1993. DONALD TRUMP'S AGE IS NOT RECEIVING THE SAME 'SCRUTINY' AS BIDEN'S DID, ATLANTIC WRITER COMPLAINS Behar said Trump’s humor has changed significantly since she knew him as a New York celebrity decades ago. "I knew him when he was just an annoying New York figure," she said. "Back then, he had a sense of humor that was not as bizarre as it is now. Now his sense of humor is making fun of handicapped people." "The View" co-host recalled her earlier interactions with Trump, including a time in which she compared Trump to Woody Allen after he said that he would date his daughter Ivanka if they were not related. "He actually thought that was funny," Behar said. articles.title: Blackburn on AI Kendrick Lamar clip backlash: It wasn’t ‘intended to offend’
articles.summary: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) is defending herself after coming under fire for sharing a video, which seemed to be AI-generated, in which she appeared in the place of rapper Kendrick Lamar during his 2025 Super Bowl LIX Halftime Show performance. In a clip Fox 13 Memphis’ Rob Sneed posted to Instagram Friday, the reporter asked…
articles.body:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) is defending herself after coming under fire for sharing a video , which seemed to be AI-generated, in which she appeared in the place of rapper Kendrick Lamar during his 2025 Super Bowl LIX Halftime Show performance.

In a clip Fox 13 Memphis’ Rob Sneed posted to Instagram Friday, the reporter asked Blackburn about the viral moment, to which the lawmaker responded saying someone else had made the original video, and her campaign team shared it because she thought it was “fun.”

“It was a video that a county commissioner had created, and I thought it was just something that was fun,” Blackburn said.

Blackburn faced criticism online for sharing the likely AI-generated video, showing her dancing to Lamar’s popular song, “Not Like Us” — which he performed during the Super Bowl. Other Tennessee politicians appear as her background dancers, including Rep. Tim Burchett (R) and Sen. Bill Haggerty (R).

As of Saturday afternoon, the video has over 2.2 million views on social platform X.

Commenters generally responded negatively to the video, including former Rep. Adam Kinzinger (R-Ill.), who said, “Boomer thinks AI makes her look cool.” Other users simply called the video “cringe.”

The Tennessee senator has advocated against AI deepfake videos in the past, and she introduced a bill to protect the likeness of creators from being used without their consent.

Sneed also pressed Blackburn on another concern surrounding the video: that it could have offended Black Americans. The song, which famously includes disses against fellow rapper Drake, is often interpreted as a commentary on the appropriation of Black artists’ work.

“There would never be any action that was intended to offend,” Blackburn responded.

Blackburn is running for Tennessee governor against Democrat Jerri Green. Green responded to her opponent’s video on X.

“When I say please stop using AI to support our campaign, this is what I mean…,” Green wrote.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Blackburn a 94 percent chance to win Tennessee gubernatorial race. The state has not elected a Democrat to serve as its governor since 2006.

articles.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump-Zelensky feud escalates; Controversies hit White House before midterms
articles.summary: President Trump’s new executive order on Friday evening sparked a new wave of bipartisan backlash to his administration’s recent easing of Russian sanctions. The order halted the implementation of new penalties on Russia set to go into effect under a sweeping legislative package signed into law by the president last month. It followed Trump’s controversial…
articles.body:
President Trump’s new executive order on Friday evening sparked a new wave of bipartisan backlash to his administration’s recent easing of Russian sanctions.

The order halted the implementation of new penalties on Russia set to go into effect under a sweeping legislative package signed into law by the president last month.

It followed Trump’s controversial decision last week to temporarily lift restrictions on the sale of Russian diesel in the U.S. and in the world marketplace amid global fuel shortages.

The Trump administration has been under pressure ahead of the midterm elections to address rising fuel costs in the U.S. amid the ongoing Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright is set to join both CNN’s “State of the Union” and ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday amid blowback over these relief actions.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), who is running in Michigan’s tight Senate race, told reporters last week he did not agree with Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports into the country.

“No, not in importing it from Russia,” the GOP nominee said at the time. “I’ve actually called for a temporary export ban just to try to give some relief while farmers are out harvesting.”

Rogers will join CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday.

Less than 20 days out from the November elections, both parties are seeking to drum up support among their base in battleground states.

Former President Obama is set to travel to Ohio and Michigan next week to stump for Democratic candidates in the states. Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said it was an “ honor ” to receive Obama’s support in his competitive race against Rogers.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who recently made a $1 million donation to El-Sayed’s campaign, stumped for the Democratic candidate in Michigan this week. The New York lawmaker is set to join Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson at a town hall on Thursday.

Jackson will appear on “State of the Union” this Sunday.

Meanwhile, Trump is set to make campaign stops in seven states in the span of seven days next week, including Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) faces an uphill battle this election cycle, with the Democratic Party expected to regain control of the House.

Democrats had a 77 percent chance of retaking the lower chamber of Congress, according to Decision Desk HQ’s election forecaster on Saturday. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, shifted their predictions in 18 House races toward Democrats last week.

Johnson will join Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures” this weekend to discuss the upcoming elections. Cook Political Report publisher and editor-in-chief Amy Walter will appear on “This Week.”

Ahead of the November elections, a number of federal lawmakers and state election officials reported this week that their offices received “suspicious packages.” Several offices were evacuated after staff discovered unidentified white powder in envelopes.

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said on Friday that law enforcement intercepted a suspicious mailing before its intended destination of one of his offices in Oklahoma.

“Those who pulled this stunt should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” he wrote on social media . “If this was an attempt to intimidate or cause me to no longer use the mail as a way to stay connected with Oklahomans, it has definitely failed.”

The Oklahoma Republican will appear on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” this Sunday.

Additionally, national news this week was dominated by several high-profile staffing changes within the Trump administration.

Newly-appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia announced the departure of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle during her first press briefing on Tuesday only to step down from her role only three days later.

Zacharia faced a barrage of questioning over her legal background, after it was discovered she had not passed the bar exam despite identifying herself as a lawyer in media appearances.

Trump told Fox News’s senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy that he was not in a rush to fill the vacancy.

Additionally, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced Friday she was no longer serving as the Trump administration’s special envoy to the “Shield of the Americas” coalition.

Noem said in a statement shared on social media that the position was “always a six-month appointment” and that she remains a senior adviser at the State Department.

articles.title: O que Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro mais falaram na propaganda no rádio | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento do g1 mostra os temas mais citados nas inserções de rádio dos dois candidatos à Presidência da República.
articles.summary: Levantamento do g1 reuniu os cinco termos mais mencionados nas inserções dos candidatos à Presidência da República neste 2º turno durante a propaganda no rádios.
articles.body:
Levantamento do g1 com base nas inserções de propaganda eleitoral de Lula (PT) e de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) na rádio durante o segundo turno mostra que as campanhas concentraram as estratégias em ataques ao respectivo adversário e em temas como "mudança" e o "fim da escala 6x1".

Os termos mais mencionados na campanha de Flávio são "Brasil", com 29 menções; "Flávio", com 22 ocorrências; e "Lula", com 18.

Ranking de palavras e expressões mencionadas nas inserções de rádio de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). — Foto: Arte g1

Já a campanha de Lula focou as menções em "Lula", com 23 ocorrências; "Flávio", com 16, e "fim da escala 6x1", com 15.

Ranking de palavras e expressões mencionadas nas inserções de rádio de Lula (PT). — Foto: Arte g1

As peças analisadas estão registradas no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) e foram transmitidas entre os dias 8 e 15 de outubro.

📻📺 No segundo turno, a propaganda eleitoral gratuita no rádio e na TV se divide entre o horário eleitoral, que é exibido por 10 minutos de segunda-feira a sábado, e as inserções, que são distribuídas ao longo da programação e podem ter duração entre 30 segundos e 1 minuto.

Ao total, Flávio apresentou 15 inserções inéditas, com 1.199 palavras. Lula registrou 17 inserções, sendo 10 originais e 7 repetidas. Foram 1.415 palavras nas peças. A análise desconsiderou conectivos gramaticais, artigos, preposições e verbos sem contexto.

Na transcrição das propagandas dos candidatos, as menções ao próprio nome e ao número de urna dos candidatos vêm no contexto da campanha, como "Vote Lula, vote 13" ou "Flávio 22".

Menções refletem estratégias das campanhas

A prevalência, pela parte de Lula, de menções a Flávio nas propagandas vem ao encontro da estratégia definida pela coordenação da campanha neste 2º turno.

Após focar no legado do último mandato nas propagandas do 1º turno e ter ficado atrás do adversário do PL, a equipe de Lula recalculou a rota e passou a explorar o temor que uma eventual eleição de Flávio pode causar em parte do eleitorado.

Segundo pesquisa Quaest divulgada na quarta-feira (14), o medo da volta da família Bolsonaro ao poder empata com o medo da reeleição de Lula, com 43% cada.

Já a campanha de Flávio quer reforçar o discurso de "mudança" no 2º turno e buscar o apoio de eleitores insatisfeitos com o governo Lula. "O Brasil quer mudança" tornou-se o principal mote do candidato do PL em discursos e propagandas.

Aliados de Flávio haviam sinalizado que, nesta etapa final da campanha, a propaganda seria dedicada às propostas do candidato . Integrantes da equipe avaliam que a estratégia de explorar temas do cotidiano e focar em temas como endividamento, inflação e violência urbana nas peças do 1º turno funcionou.

O fim da escala 6x1, promulgada na sexta (16), também se tornou um tema estratégico para os dois candidatos nesta reta final de campanha. Enquanto Lula teve a pauta como uma das principais bandeiras da candidatura, Flávio se opunha à proposta, propondo uma discussão sobre a contratação por hora de trabalho.

Diante da pressão pela aprovação, o candidato do PL mudou de posição e votou a favor da proposta no Senado, que teve apenas 1 voto contrário — o do senador Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS), ex-vice de Jair Bolsonaro.

Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) durante propaganda eleitoral gratuita nesta quarta-feira (14). — Foto: Reprodução

articles.title: Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro no Instagram: levantamento mostra estratégias | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento do g1 com mais de 2 mil posts até outubro mostra que o presidente apostou em volume na campanha e aumento nas menções ao adversário no segundo turno, enquanto o senador alcançou mais gente com cada publicação e centrou discurso em pedidos de voto.
articles.summary: Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro no Instagram mudam táticas no segundo turno, com foco em ataques diretos e mobilização de votos em busca de maior engajamento digital.
articles.body:
O presidente Lula ( PT ) e o senador Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) chegam à reta final da eleição usando o Instagram de formas diferentes, e em papéis invertidos em relação ao começo do ano.

Na pré-campanha, Flávio publicava mais, tinha mais engajamento e era o único a atacar o adversário. Na campanha, em agosto, Lula assumiu a dianteira em volume de publicações e, no segundo turno, passou a falar mais diretamente do rival. Flávio publica menos, mas seus posts tiveram maior alcance, e a mensagem segue girando em torno de duas palavras: “vote” e “vencer”.

O g1 analisou 2.129 publicações dos perfis @lulaoficial e @flaviobolsonaro no Instagram, a rede social mais declarada pelos candidatos nas eleições deste ano ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) , entre 1º de janeiro e 14 de outubro de 2026. São 1.305 da pré-campanha, até 15 de agosto, e 824 da campanha, que começou em 16 de agosto. Os dados foram coletados em outubro, e a análise considera as métricas de curtidas, comentários e reproduções, além dos textos das legendas dos posts.

A mudança mais visível está nas legendas do presidente. De janeiro a meados de agosto, quando a campanha começou oficialmente, Lula não citou “Bolsonaro” nem “Flávio” em nenhum post. No mesmo período, Flávio mencionou “Lula” em 21% das publicações, e “governo Lula” estava entre suas expressões mais frequentes.

No primeiro turno, o nome do adversário passou a aparecer em cerca de 4% dos posts de Lula. No segundo turno, “Bolsonaro” está em 26% das publicações, e “Flávio”, em 20%. “Flávio Bolsonaro” virou a expressão de duas palavras mais usada pelo presidente nessa fase, presente em 20 posts, à frente de “povo brasileiro” (16). Um vídeo de 8 de outubro que começa com “O Brasil perde com Flávio Bolsonaro” teve 22,3 milhões de reproduções.

Com isso, as posições se inverteram. Flávio, que citava Lula em um a cada cinco posts na pré-campanha, reduziu a proporção para 18% no primeiro turno e 15% no segundo. Mas os posts de confronto do senador são diretos e estão entre os que mais rendem.

Em 14 de outubro, o candidato do PL publicou um vídeo dirigido a Lula, em que anuncia que vai participar do debate realizado pela TV Bandeirantes, neste domingo (18), e diz "vou esfregar a verdade na tua cara”. O vídeo teve 26,2 milhões de reproduções, o mais visto do senador no segundo turno. Um dia antes de postar esse vídeo, Flávio Bolsonaro havia dito que não participaria do debate.

As palavras mais usadas nas legendas de posts dos candidatos — Foto: Alberto Correia - Arte/g1

Nessa sexta-feira (16), reportagem publicada pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo informou que, em mensagens internas, funcionários da Meta, dona do Instagram, reconheceram restrições que prejudicaram contas de Lula na rede social.

Em nota, a empresa negou ter tomado medidas para interferir nas eleições e afirmou que houve uma falha técnica em 7 de outubro que afetou a plataforma no mundo todo, não apenas no Brasil. "Durante cerca de cinco horas, as contagens de visualizações ficaram congeladas, incorretas ou zeradas, embora o conteúdo continuasse sendo distribuído normalmente. O incidente afetou criadores em mais de 100 países", informou a empresa.

Levantamento mostra posts no Instagram nos perfis oficiais de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: Arte g1

O vocabulário de Lula no Instagram também mudou ao longo do ano. Na pré-campanha, o presidente falava como governo. As palavras que mais o distinguiam de Flávio Bolsonaro eram “indústria”, “programa”, “estudantes”, “Mercosul” e “trabalhando”. Entre as expressões mais usadas estavam “União Europeia”, “novo PAC” e “inteligência artificial”.

No primeiro turno, ganharam espaço termos como “oportunidades”, “educação”, “garantir”, “bets” e “pronto”. A proibição das apostas esportivas por medida provisória rendeu um dos posts mais curtidos do presidente na campanha, em 25 de setembro, com 1,6 milhão de interações.

No segundo turno, o tom mudou para fomentar a mobilização de eleitores do petista. “Bora” foi de 2% para 18% dos posts, e “família”, de 10% para 19%. “Povo”, termo mais frequente de Lula depois de “Brasil”, subiu de 30% para 37%.

O fim da escala 6x1, aprovado pelo Senado na quarta-feira (14) , virou bandeira: “6x1” aparece em 12% das publicações do segundo turno, contra 4% no primeiro. O post sobre a aprovação da proposta, de 14 de outubro, teve 2,7 milhões de curtidas e comentários e é o segundo de maior engajamento de Lula na campanha. Perderam espaço palavras como “soberania” e “bets”.

Flávio Bolsonaro já falava como candidato desde a pré-campanha. As palavras mais típicas dele no período eram “Bolsonaro”, “resgatar”, “esquerda”, “master” e “Flávio”. “Vamos resgatar” era sua expressão mais frequente.

Na campanha, o discurso se concentrou no voto. “Vote” aparece em 57% dos posts do senador no primeiro turno e em 54% no segundo. “Vencer” está em 49% e 50%, respectivamente. No primeiro turno, as palavras que mais o distinguiam de Lula foram “libertar”, “vencer”, “turno”, “vote” e “primeiro”.

No fim do primeiro turno, posts que citam o termo "censura" dominaram as publicações de maior alcance do senador, como “a censura não irá vencer!” (1º de outubro) e “censura nunca mais!” (2 de outubro). No segundo turno, o post com mais engajamento trata do fato de que o programa eleitoral dele foi exibido sem som na televisão (2,3 milhões de interações), o que aconteceu no dia 12 de outubro. “Mudança” passou de 7% para 12% das publicações.

Postagem de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) com maior engajamento no segundo turno até 15 de outubro — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Mudança de discurso acompanha explosão de publicações

Na pré-campanha, Flávio publicou 804 posts, média de 24,8 por semana, contra 501 de Lula — 15,4 por semana. O senador manteve entre 92 e 130 posts por mês até julho. Lula só acelerou em julho, quando publicou 101 posts, contra 56 em junho. A partir da semana de 27 de julho, passou a postar mais que o adversário e não perdeu mais a dianteira.

Na campanha, a diferença se ampliou. Lula manteve o ritmo de 10,3 posts por dia nos dois turnos, mais que o triplo de Flávio. O senador caiu de 3,4 para 2,4 posts diários no segundo turno, redução de 30%.

A virada no volume também inverteu o engajamento total. Na pré-campanha, os posts de Flávio somaram 146,1 milhões de curtidas e comentários, contra 58,3 milhões dos de Lula. Na campanha, Lula soma 182,1 milhões, e Flávio, 81,8 milhões. No segundo turno, o presidente acumula 8,4 milhões de interações por dia, e o senador, 2 milhões.

Post a post, Flávio leva vantagem durante quase todo o ano. Na pré-campanha, a publicação típica do senador (a mediana) rendeu 109 mil curtidas e comentários, mais que o dobro das 51 mil de Lula. No primeiro turno, foram 167 mil para Flávio e 94 mil para Lula. No segundo turno, o engajamento dos dois disparou e ficou próximo: 680 mil para Lula e 658 mil para Flávio.

Os posts de Lula no segundo turno também provocam muito mais conversa. São 161 comentários para cada mil curtidas, contra 62 na pré-campanha e 63 no primeiro turno. Para Flávio, a taxa ficou estável: 60 comentários para cada mil curtidas na pré-campanha, depois 65 no primeiro turno e 69 no segundo.

O quadro se inverteu com a oficialização das candidaturas, no início de agosto. A partir daí, o perfil de Lula no Instagram passou a publicar 68 posts por semana em média, cinco vezes o ritmo do primeiro semestre, e chegou a 357 posts em setembro.

Flávio manteve os 24 posts por semana. Em setembro, Lula publicou quase quatro vezes mais que o senador (357 a 94).

Flávio Bolsonaro sempre priorizou vídeos: foram 90% dos posts na pré-campanha, 94% no primeiro turno e 96% no segundo. Lula começou o ano com uma mistura de formatos, com 47% de vídeos e 40% de carrosséis, muitos com fotos de Ricardo Stuckert (fotógrafo oficial do presidente), citado em 296 legendas na pré-campanha. Na campanha, a proporção de vídeos do presidente subiu para 64% no primeiro turno e 81% no segundo.

Postagens no Instagram dos candidatos, por formato — Foto: Arte/g1

Nas reproduções, o vídeo típico de Flávio teve 1,2 milhão na pré-campanha, 2,1 milhões no primeiro turno e 6,9 milhões no segundo. O de Lula teve 1 milhão, 1,5 milhão e 6,5 milhões.

O vídeo mais reproduzido da campanha é de Lula: “O seu voto decide qual será o caminho do Brasil”, de 10 de outubro, com 39,9 milhões. O de Flávio é o agradecimento “OBRIGADO, BRASIL!”, de 3 de outubro, com 36,8 milhões.

O post com mais curtidas e comentários do ano é o pronunciamento de Flávio após o resultado do primeiro turno, em 4 de outubro , após superar Lula por uma diferença de 2,2 milhões de votos: foram 3,5 milhões de interações.

O melhor desempenho de Lula no Instagram foi um vídeo de 7 de outubro que convoca os eleitores para o segundo turno, com 2,8 milhões de interações.

Na pré-campanha, os recordes foram um vídeo de Flávio com críticas a Lula no carnaval, em 16 de fevereiro (2,3 milhões), e o lançamento do “Rap do Silva” por Lula, em 26 de julho (1,3 milhão).

Postagem de Lula no Instagram — Foto: Arte/g1

Foram coletadas as legendas dos perfis @lulaoficial e @flaviobolsonaro, incluindo posts em que um deles aparece como coautor. As publicações foram divididas em pré-campanha (de 1º de janeiro até 15 de agosto), primeiro turno (16 de agosto a 4 de outubro) e segundo turno (a partir de 5 de outubro).

Na análise dos posts, foram descartadas palavras sem conteúdo, como artigos e preposições.

O engajamento de um post é calculado somando curtidas e comentários .

Mediana: o "post típico" é a mediana, valor que divide os posts ao meio e não é distorcido por virais.

Palavras: as palavras mais típicas de cada perfil foram medidas pela razão de chances logarítmicas entre as frequências nos dois perfis. O aviso legal de propaganda eleitoral, repetido em centenas de legendas, foi removido antes da análise.

Limitações . Só o texto das legendas foi analisado, não o que é dito nos vídeos. Curtidas, comentários e visualizações continuam crescendo depois da coleta, então os posts de outubro estão subestimados. O segundo turno ainda está em curso, e a amostra dessa fase é pequena. Poucos posts a mais podem mudar a ordem das palavras.

Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula. — Foto: Foto: Mateus Bonomi/Reuters; Roberto Sungi/Estadão Conteúdo

articles.title: Davi Alcolumbre articula reeleição no Senado com Lula ou Flávio | G1
articles.standfirst: Principal estratégia é rachar os votos no próprio PL. Apesar de contar com uma bancada de quase 30 parlamentares, alguns senadores da sigla são do grupo político de Alcolumbre.
articles.summary: Davi Alcolumbre articula sua reeleição no Senado e negocia apoios para se manter no comando do Congresso em 2027 sob qualquer governo.
articles.body:
O presidente do Senado Federal , Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), já trabalha para ser reeleito para a presidência da Casa em 2027, seja em um governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) ou do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ).

As declarações do presidente do PL, Valdemar Costa Neto , de que o partido não apoiará sua reeleição e lançará Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) como candidato fez Alcolumbre intensificar sua campanha.

O Partido Liberal elegeu 19 novos senadores nas Eleições de 2026 e terá uma bancada de 29 cadeiras no Senado Federal em 2026.

Na última semana, o presidente do Senado fez movimentos em favor de pautas do interesse do governo Lula, com destaque para a aprovação da PEC que acaba com a escala 6x1.

A disputa pública com Rogério Marinho teve início na quinta-feira (15) no plenário do Senado quando os dois bateram boca após Alcolumbre retirar a PEC da Segurança da pauta de análise dos senadores.

“A retirada de pauta se deveu ao pedido do governo?” , questionou Marinho .

“Não, a retirada de pauta se deveu à minha decisão da Presidência do Senado Federal” , respondeu Alcolumbre.

“Mas eu pergunto à vossa excelência: baseada em quê? Porque há uma expectativa da população” , insistiu Marinho.

"Baseado na decisão da presidência do Senado Federal" , rebateu Alcolumbre.

"O arbítrio é de vossa excelência, pura e simplesmente?" , questionou Marinho.

"Bom saber que a gente precisa mudar esse regimento" , pontuou Marinho.

"Exatamente. Vamos mudar" , finalizou Alcolumbre.

A principal estratégia de Alcolumbre é rachar os votos no próprio PL. Apesar de contar com uma bancada de quase 30 parlamentares, alguns desses senadores fazem parte do grupo político de Alcolumbre, como o senador Eduardo Gomes (PL-TO), vice-presidente do Senado.

Segundo aliados, o primeiro movimento de Alcolumbre deve envolver justamente Eduardo Gomes. Ele deve ser escolhido como relator do Orçamento de 2027, que ainda não começou a ser discutido pelo Congresso Nacional.

A relatoria do Orçamento do ano que vem ficaria com um senador do MDB por um acordo político já definido, mas a escolha de Gomes é uma sinalização aos senadores do PL.

Alcolumbre tem dito a interlocutores que o PL tem toda a legitimidade para lançar Marinho ou qualquer outro quadro como candidato, mas lembra que o partido sofreu uma derrota na eleição passada, quando enfrentou o grupo do atual presidente do Senado na eleição da Mesa Diretora.

Em 2023, Marinho concorreu contra o então senador Rodrigo Pacheco na disputa pela presidência e acabou derrotado por 49 votos a 32. Como consequência, o partido ficou dois anos sem o comando de nenhuma comissão na Casa e sem espaço na Mesa Diretora.

Em 2025, o PL não correu o mesmo risco e apoiou Davi Alcolumbre.

Aliados de Alcolumbre calculam que ele tem ao menos os mesmos 49 votos que Pacheco teve em 2023. Outros interlocutores fazem uma projeção mais apertada, com 44 votos.

Além disso, diante do crescimento do PL, lideranças de outros partidos tem articulado uma união das outras siglas em torno do nome de Alcolumbre.

Na terça-feira (13), Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM) e Otto Alencar (PSD-BA), líderes de MDB e PSD, respectivamente, anunciaram que apoiarão a reeleição de Alcolumbre.

"Eu tive a oportunidade de exercer o meu voto favorável à sua Presidência e posso exercê-lo de novo pelo trabalho, pela sua perseverança, pela sua presença no Senado Federal discutindo as matérias", afirmou Alencar.

A avaliação dos partidos é que um eventual governo Flávio Bolsonaro com o PL presidindo a Casa tiraria a independência do Congresso e poderia retirar dos parlamentares sua principal fonte de poder: as emendas parlamentares.

Nos bastidores, Alcolumbre é conhecido por operar as emendas e sempre esticar a corda com o governo federal para defender o interesse dos parlamentares.

Presidente do Senado Federal, senador Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP) — Foto: Waldemir Barreto/Agência Senado

Nas últimas semanas, Alcolumbre ouviu quase todos os novos senadores eleitos e tem tratado diariamente das negociações para acomodar os novatos em gabinetes e apartamentos funcionais que escolherem.

Além de receber os novatos, Alcolumbre também conversa com os senadores que estão no meio do mandato ou que foram reeleitos e buscam novos gabinetes e apartamentos.

Os gabinetes mais disputados ficam no Anexo II do Senado e tem um acesso reservado ao estacionamento que possibilita entrar e sair sem chamar a atenção. Um desses gabinetes foi visitado 18 vezes em um único dia.

Outro gabinete, ocupado pelo senador Jorge Kajuru (PSB-GO), na ala dos plenários onde aconteceram as sessões da CPMI do INSS já foi visitado por quase duas dezenas de novos parlamentares. O espaço tem como diferencial o acesso a uma entrada lateral restrita do Senado Federal.

Questionado pelo g1 sobre a dança das cadeiras nos gabinetes do Senado, Alcolumbre disse que já conversou "com quase todos" os novatos.

Segundo aliados, Alcolumbre tem trabalhado para acomodar até adversários em um bom gabinete, como a senadora eleita Rayssa Furlan (PSD-AP), que derrotou os candidatos de Alcolumbre ao Senado no Amapá.

Nas negociações entram também dezenas de cargos vinculados à presidência do Senado que podem ser ocupados por indicados de aliados de Davi.

Contrário ao impeachment de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), principalmente em relação ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes, de quem é próximo, Alcolumbre não desistiu de emplacar o ministro do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU), Rodrigo Pacheco no STF.

Pacheco sempre foi o nome defendido por Alcolumbre junto a Lula e a não escolha do ex-colega foi o motivo que levou o presidente do Senado a articular a rejeição de Jorge Messias, Advogado-Geral da União (AGU), no Senado.

Aliados veem a manobra de Alcolumbre como um recado tanto a Lula quanto a Flávio Bolsonaro.

No caso de Lula, nomear Pacheco seria uma forma de, ganhando ou perdendo, garantir uma indicação para a Suprema Corte. Caso seja derrotado, o presidente deixaria para o sucessor três vagas no STF em vez de quatro.

Com Flávio eleito, a nomeação de Pacheco garantiria a Alcolumbre um aliado de primeira hora no Supremo caso a pressão pelo impeachment de Alexandre de Moraes se torne insustentável.

Além disso, a ida de Pacheco ao STF abriria novamente uma vaga do Senado no TCU, o que poderia ser utilizado por Alcolumbre nas negociações de apoio para sua reeleição na Casa.

Parlamentares contrários à reeleição de Alcolumbre avaliam que a vaga no TCU poderia ir para o próprio caso ele não consiga se manter na presidência do Senado.

articles.title: Sen. Graham on Trump waiving Russia sanctions: ‘I look forward to talking to him’
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) said Saturday that she would prefer to keep sanctions pressure on Russia after President Trump waived sanctions on the country that were enacted through a bill Graham championed. Trump signed an executive order Friday waiving sanctions on Russian energy, passed under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. The…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) said Saturday that she would prefer to keep sanctions pressure on Russia after President Trump waived sanctions on the country that were enacted through a bill Graham championed.

Trump signed an executive order Friday waiving sanctions on Russian energy, passed under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. The measures were intended to apply increased pressure on the U.S. adversary to end its war in Ukraine.

Graham championed the bill, which was named for her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The South Carolina senator told the Associated Press Saturday that she is proud of the legislation, but did not go as far as other GOP officials in bashing the president’s order.

“The president and I share the same goal, which is to end the war, get gas and diesel prices down,” Graham said. “The sanctions bill is one of the tools he can use to do that. It’s up to him whether or not he chooses to use it.”

“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia … because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” she added.

Graham’s brother Lindsey fought to pass tougher sanctions on Russia just before his death earlier this year, and the bill named in his honor passed with overwhelming bipartisan support. Graham said Saturday that the bill “meant a lot to Lindsey,” but that he at times disagreed with the president.

“They had that relationship where they could agree to disagree sometimes,” Graham said.

Members of both parties blasted the president’s decision over the weekend. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost renomination after Trump endorsed his opponent, said in a post to the social platform X, “Lindsey would be appalled.”

While Graham did not criticize the president directly, she did say she was likely to discuss the matter with him when he visits South Carolina for a rally next week.

“I look forward to talking to him next week because he’s gonna be in the state, so we’ll probably sit down and, you know, we’ll talk about this,” Graham said.

articles.title: Minnesota Senate race takes bizarre turn after dark family history uncovered
articles.summary: Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan's grandfather spent decades in psychiatric custody and was suspected in multiple killings, records show.
articles.body: A dark chapter in the family history of Minnesota Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan has made its way into the race, but it is unclear whether voters will hold the alleged sins of her long-dead grandfather against her. Earlier this week, Alpha News revealed the troubled mental health history of Flanagan's grandfather, John Jacob Hartmann, supported by old newspaper accounts and court records. He spent decades in psychiatric custody, escaped twice and was suspected in multiple killings, though never charged. The reporting comes just weeks before the midterm elections, in which Flanagan, the state's lieutenant governor, faces former television sports reporter Michelle Tafoya in a race to fill the seat of Democrat Tina Smith, who is retiring. Neither Flanagan nor Tafoya has commented publicly on the matter since the decades-old allegations resurfaced. But the bizarre development has generated a buzz on social media. Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet highlighted the "violent mental illness in Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan's family," in an X post, followed by a photo of Flanagan wearing a shirt that says "Protect trans kids." and Dustin Grage, a columnist with Town Hall, wrote the report "adds up." Flanagan has frequently spoken about her upbringing, including being raised by a single mother who relied on SNAP benefits and housing assistance, and the influence of her indigenous father, a tribal land rights activist who helped inspire her own advocacy for Native American communities. But a lesser-known part of her family history involves Hartmann, who made headlines in Minneapolis newspapers throughout the 1970s and early 1980s for his time in psychiatric hospitals, his escapes and allegations linking him to at least four killings, which was dredged up by Minnesota-based outlet Alpha News. WARREN’S ANCESTRY SAGA ROARS BACK AFTER DEM ALLY TOUTS NATIVE SENATE FIRST: ‘ARROWS FIRED’ Flanagan was three years old when Hartmann died on Feb. 6, 1983. A Minnesota Star Tribune death notice listed Flanagan’s mother, Patricia Hartmann, and her three sisters — Kathleen, Mary and Margaret — as his surviving daughters. An obituary for Patricia, who died in 2022, listed her maiden name as Hartmann and identified her father as John. In an interview with Minnesota Women’s Press, Flanagan said both her mother and grandmother were single mothers. She described her grandmother as having raised four daughters "at a time when that didn’t happen a lot." Flanagan's mother eventually married Thomas Flanagan, who is identified as Peggy Flanagan's stepfather in his obituary. In a Feb. 9, 1983 article announcing Hartmann's death, the newspaper now known as The Minnesota Star Tribune stated that he was committed on Nov. 1, 1951 after his wife filed a petition claiming that he was "mentally ill and dangerous." His commitment came after the body of a man named Theodore Foth was found burning in his room, although Hartmann was never charged in Foth's death. The paper also named Hartmann as a suspect in a 1964 murder of a fellow patient at the Minnesota Security Hospital, but he was never charged. SLEEPER GOP CANDIDATE PUTS BLUE-LEANING STATE IN PLAY AS FRAUD SCANDAL SHADOWS DEMS Hartmann was transferred to Anoka State Hospital in 1970, but escaped to New Mexico, where the newspaper reported he was suspected in the deaths of a man and woman. However, a 1973 Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals ruling does not mention the alleged murder allegations against Hartmann. Instead, the ruling stated New Mexico authorities picked up Hartmann from a warrant issued by Minnesota Probate Judge Melvin Peterson in September 1970. The authorities found that he was living in the state "without incident and without hiding his identity following his escape in Minnesota." A special prosecutor later released Hartmann, finding that he was "sane and safe to be at large." Hartmann was apprehended in Colorado for a misdemeanor charge the next year and brought back to Minnesota. In April 1979, Hartmann failed to return from a visit pass at the Minnesota Security Hospital and fled to Missouri, where he allegedly threatened U.S. District Judge Miles Welton Lord during a phone call. Lord presided over Hartmann’s earlier federal challenge to his involuntary return from Colorado to Minnesota and initially dismissed claims against several Minnesota officials. Hartmann was charged by federal authorities for the alleged threat, according to a 1979 Star Tribune article. articles.title: Three takeaways from Elon Musk's latest political donations
articles.summary: New filings show the world's richest person spent this summer again trying to help Republicans win office, with most of his focus on one candidate.
articles.body:
Billionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk is once again pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into a US election - this time with the aim of helping Republicans maintain their control of Congress.

Musk donated upwards of $200m (£150m) in the quarter that ended on 30 September, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings reviewed by the BBC.

The fillings were released with just over two weeks until the 2026 midterm election, where many races for the House of Representatives and Senate are close and Republicans risk losing their majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate.

Musk also put significant money, $290m, and effort into helping elect President Donald Trump and other Republicans in 2024.

Here is where the richest person in the world has been donating this time around, and what it might mean for his businesses.

The bulk of the money donated last quarter by the world's only trillionaire, $158m, went to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) Pac, the filings showed.

It is one of the largest publicly known single political donations in US history, and some have suggested it is the biggest ever.

SLF is a super Pac backing Republican Senate candidates in tough races.

It quickly sent the money on to a group supporting Texas Republican Ken Paxton. The state attorney general, Paxton is at risk of losing to Democrat James Talarico in a race for a seat his party has held for decades. They have been polling neck and neck and the election's outcome is considered a bellwether for the future of Republican power.

Super Pacs are independent "political action committees" that can raise unlimited amounts of money and play a major role in funding US political campaigns.

Musk also donated more than $80m to the America Pac that he founded during the 2024 election.

America Pac last quarter spent millions on digital communications, mailings and phone calls opposing Talarico, as well as thousands on political marketing to support Paxton.

At the same time, Musk donated another $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, a group primarily backing Paxton, records show.

The flow of money highlights a major theme for Musk: Texas.

In recent years, the tech CEO has been moving his business empire - including SpaceX, Tesla and X - to the southern US state after expressing frustration with operating in California.

Texas has offered Musk fewer government regulations and no state personal income tax and no corporate income tax.

Keeping politicians who favour looser government restrictions in charge, as Republicans typically have, could help maintain that environment for Musk.

And his big spending in Texas and in the Texas Senate race seems to point to Musk's understanding of that, political analyst Cayce Myers told the BBC.

"Republicans have a fundraising advantage this time, but fundraising by itself does not actually guarantee success," he said.

For many voters this year, technology has become a top issue. People across the country are pushing for increased government oversight of artificial intelligence, data centres and social media.

That's something that has tech leaders like Musk developing closer ties to the Republican party, which historically has promoted lighter government regulation, Myers said.

"What [tech leaders] are looking at is a future where there is growing demand and call for regulation and I think they want to be in an advantageous position," he said. "We're seeing them shift, and fall behind Republicans."

Other tech leaders, such as OpenAI president and his wife Greg and Anna Brockman are also putting big money behind Republicans.

The couple donated $25m to the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc Pac last year.

Myer noted it's not just the tech sector, but industries like cryptocurrency and gambling where large sums of money are being donated in an attempt to exert influence.

"This is the idea of shaping the regulatory environment through contributions," he said.

articles.title: ‘No Kings’ protesters spurn organizers' rules: ‘This is as partisan as you can get’
articles.summary: Protesters at official No Kings events openly urged voters to "vote blue" and elect Democrats, directly contradicting organizers' nonpartisan rules.
articles.body: ALEXANDRIA, Va. — On South Washington Street, 26-year-old environmental engineer Nayely Cruz Hernandez had a straightforward message for voters as she joined a phalanx of protesters lining the street for nationwide "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump: "Vote blue." "We got to take the power away from Trump, from the Republicans," Hernandez told Fox News Digital. "So we got to win the House, we got to win the Senate, not only in Virginia, but across the country." Standing beside her boyfriend, Noah Schwarzott, 25, their 13-year-old Maltese-poodle, Maybellene, in her arms, Hernandez acknowledged that national No Kings organizers had their own rules for the protests to be "nonpartisan," but she wasn't following orders. 'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS "The No King ... organizers can say whatever," she said. "But I'm saying vote blue, because why are we here? Who's in the House? Who's in the Senate? Who is the President? It's red, it's Republicans, and it's Trump." A Fox News Digital investigation documented about 300 organizations with $2.5 billion in combined annual revenues behind the "No Kings" protest network, including Democratic-aligned advocacy groups, major labor unions and nonprofits including MoveOn, the American Federation of Teachers and the ACLU. Cruz Hernandez ended by introducing Maybellene and declaring that the dog was "telling you to vote for Don Beyer," a Democratic member of Congress who represents Alexandria, Arlington and other Northern Virginia communities. The national organizers' position is that the Oct. 17 events must be "nonpartisan." That's to comply with the federal laws that regulate the nonprofits that fund the No Kings protests. PARTY POOPERS' FIGHT CARD: JANE FONDA, 'NO KINGS,' COMMUNISTS ROLL OUT RIVAL SPECTACLE TO TRUMP'S 250TH Her comments directly contradicted the written instructions of the national "No Kings" organization and its leaders at the Indivisible nonprofit, prohibiting calls to "vote Blue," elect Democrats or endorse candidates and target individuals. Nearby, a man held a sign by a far-left group called "Refuse Fascism" with another message defying the organizers' guidance: "TRUMP MUST GO NOW!" Another man held an inflatable balloon mocking Trump as a baby in a diaper. Another sign said "86 47," the controversial message former FBI Director James Comey posted on social media and which federal prosecutors deemed an overt threat against Trump. As the young couple cheered honking cars, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz, national spokesperson for No Kings, called Fox News Digital to insist "No Kings" is a "nonpartisan, peaceful movement that has brought millions of Americans together to stand up for democracy, defend our freedoms, and reject authoritarianism." DAVID MARCUS: AS DEMOCRATS PROTEST IN DALLAS, CONSERVATIVES ARE QUIET AND CAUTIOUS Told that a Fox News DIgital investigation found "No Kings" events from Maine to Oregon were clearly partisan, Epstein-Ortiz said, "We are aware of partisan events circulating online that are not affiliated with or officially organized by No Kings. Many people utilize the No Kings name as a rallying cry." But, in this case, the protest on South Washington Street was an official "No Kings" event, advertised on the organizers' official website. Among the demonstrators, one woman beamed while waving a sign that was explicit about the protest's agenda: "THE USA Needs a Big Beautiful BLUE WAVE." But hours after the Alexandria demonstration, Fox News Digital encountered another protester marching on H Street NW by the White House who openly rejected the nonpartisan description. She marched at an official "No Kings" event. Nadine Seiler, a self-described "professional protester" recently mentioned by Trump, was asked whether she agreed with organizers' insistence that the demonstration was nonpartisan. "No, no, the people who agree with Trump are not out here," Seiler responded from behind an inflatable costume. "So it's never gonna be non-partisan if it's a resistance to the fascist regime." "They can pretend, but it's not," she added. Asked directly whether the event was partisan, Seiler answered: "Yes, this is a partisan protest." She explained that participants were resisting what she described as illegal policies of the Trump administration. "Yeah, so this is as partisan as you can get," she concluded. The exchanges offer a ground-level perspective on the political character of a movement whose organizers have gone to considerable lengths to insist its voter-mobilization activities are "nonpartisan." FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS "No Kings" has distributed detailed election-law guidance prohibiting partisan slogans, campaign materials, candidate endorsements and coordination with political parties. Yet the movement's own leadership has openly discussed its broader Democratic electoral objectives. During an Oct. 15 livestream, Indivisible co-founder Ezra Levin contrasted the parties' candidates. "Our candidates are quite good all around the country. Their candidates are quite trash all over the country," Levin said. In an Oct. 9 webinar, Levin explained how activists could criticize Trump while avoiding explicit Democratic endorsements. "Uh, you've got to let people connect the dots on that one," he said. Indivisible co-founder Leah Greenberg, meanwhile, described No Kings as a "nonpartisan coalition" intended to welcome participants across the political spectrum. The distinction matters legally. Individual protesters expressing partisan opinions don't automatically establish that event organizers violated election law. Tax-exempt charities also face restrictions different from those governing political advocacy groups. In yet another sign, a protester again targeted Trump, writing, "EVERY DAY I HATE HIM MORE THAN I DID THE DAY BEFORE." Another sign read: "NO CROWN FOR THE CLOWN." From northern Virginia to the White House, participants were making no effort to conceal their political preferences. For Seiler, the description was simple: "This is as partisan as you can get." articles.title: Top takeaways from JD Vance town hall: Costly gas, DC corruption, immigration hot takes and the war
articles.summary: JD Vance defended Trump administration policies on gas prices, Iran's nuclear program, and H-1B visas while blasting Abdul El-Sayed at a CBS town hall.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance faced questions from Michigan voters during a town hall in Flat Rock as the state emerges as a key battleground in the fight for Senate control in November's midterms. The town hall hosted by CBS News came just weeks before the midterm elections as Republicans are fighting to keep their majorities in the House and Senate. Vying for the open Senate seat in Michigan is Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former member of the House of Representatives. Here are the top moments from the town hall: Vance places blame on Biden administration for high gas prices The first question Vance fielded Saturday came from a 43-year-old Detroit barber, who asked him why gas prices remain significantly higher than during Trump's first term. Vance first pointed to Iran’s attacks on commercial shipping and the resulting disruption to global energy markets, but he also placed blame on the Biden administration. "That's actually the biggest reason why gas prices are so high, because when Joe Biden was president, we had about 20% of American refining capacity that went offline," Vance said. Vance said the Trump administration was using the Defense Production Act to help restore domestic refining capacity, but cautioned that rebuilding that infrastructure would take time. CBS News anchor Tony Dokoupil pushed back on Vance's attempts to blame Biden, noting that Trump and Vance have been in office for nearly two years while Americans continued to face high gas prices. MORNING GLORY: PRESIDENT TRUMP AND THE AMERICAN MILITARY HAVE BEATEN IRAN Vance pressed on White House corruption allegations Dokoupil shifted the conversation to government corruption, citing a Fox News poll showing that 60% of voters were extremely concerned about the issue. He asked Vance whether anything he had witnessed inside the Trump White House made him feel "squeamish." "You certainly see evidence of corruption in Washington, D.C. Do I see evidence of corruption from the president of the United States, from the administration? No, Tony, I just don’t," Vance said. The exchange came days after Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid allegations that she sought $100,000 from a donor seeking access to Trump administration officials. Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing. Dokoupil pressed Vance on the allegations involving Guilfoyle, along with concerns about restrictions on IRS scrutiny of Trump's tax returns and the president's cryptocurrency earnings. Vance said selling access to the White House would be "disgusting and despicable" and that anyone responsible should face consequences. Dokoupil then asked whether Vance would comply with subpoenas investigating alleged corruption if Democrats took control of Congress in January. "Of course, of course I will," Vance said. "Look, we follow the law. I follow the law." KIMBERLY GUILFOYLE FACES POTENTIAL SENATE PROBE OVER BOMBSHELL $100K ALLEGATION Vance acknowledges 'imperfect' immigration rhetoric Vance was confronted over his immigration rhetoric by a naturalized U.S. citizen who said she voted for the vice president but questioned why the administration was "scapegoating immigrants." The voter, who immigrated to the United States 20 years ago, challenged Vance over his characterization of certain H-1B visa workers as "foreign indentured servants." "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said. But Vance defended his remarks, arguing that his criticism was aimed at companies exploiting foreign workers rather than immigrants themselves. He said the H-1B visa system gives employers too much power over foreign workers whose ability to remain in the country depends on their employment, while also allowing companies to replace American workers with visa holders. "That's not a criticism of the H-1B visa holder. That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker," Vance said. Dokoupil pressed Vance on whether his rhetoric and that of the Trump administration dehumanized immigrants. "My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant. And in fact, I love a number of immigrants," Vance said. But Vance argued that allowing too many immigrants into the country too quickly could undermine social cohesion and fundamentally change American communities. "I have neighbors, I have friends of mine who literally don't know a single person in their neighborhood who speaks the language they do," Vance said. "I don't think it's unreasonable for an American citizen to want to share their community with people they have something in common with." Though the town hall was pre-recorded, Vance took to X shortly after it aired to share footage from showing a burning building in France amid mass riots. He said what's unfolding in France is a cautionary tale for the United States. "Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility," Vance posted on X. "They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen. I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn," Vance continued. Vance claims U.S. has destroyed Iran's nuclear program Dokoupil pressed Vance on why the war with Iran had dragged on longer than the Trump administration anticipated, asking the vice president, "Why haven't we won decisively?" Vance argued that the U.S. had "in some ways" already won the war, claiming that American military strikes had successfully destroyed Iran's nuclear program, which he described as the central reason Trump launched the operation. "Have we destroyed the Iranian nuclear program? The answer is yes," Vance said. But Vance said the administration was still working to secure a "long-term" and "verifiable" commitment from Iran that it would not rebuild its nuclear capabilities, while also preventing Tehran from disrupting global energy supplies. Vance said the Iranians responded by terrorizing commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting global oil supplies and driving up gas prices. He claimed gas prices would be "three times as high" if it weren't for the U.S. Navy protecting commercial shipping through the waterway. VANCE TAKES AIM AT SOFT-ON-CRIME DEMS AS GOP FACES UPHILL MIDTERM BATTLE: ‘LOST THEIR MINDS’ Vance blasts El-Sayed over synagogue attack response Vance was also urged by a Michigan voter to condemn antisemitism within his own political base, including rhetoric from prominent conservative figures such as Tucker Carlson. The question came from Eddie Rubin, a lifelong Democrat whose 5-year-old daughter and 3-year-old son survived the attack at Temple Israel, which occurred in March in Michigan. The attacker, a Lebanese-born U.S. citizen, rammed his pickup truck through the synagogue's entrance before exchanging gunfire with security. The attacker was killed, but no children or synagogue staff members were injured. "I condemn anti-Semitism. I condemn Jew hatred," Vance said. But Vance also turned the conversation to Michigan's Senate race, criticizing Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for his response to the synagogue attack. Vance pointed to El-Sayed's remark that "hurt people hurt people." "He went around and said, 'hurt people, hurt people', showing empathy, not with you and your family, which is where I think that we got to show empathy. But showing empathy to a guy who nearly killed hundreds of innocent children," Vance said. articles.title: Michigan Democrat confirms sister-in-law's terror watchlist lawsuit days before Obama campaign appearance
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged his sister-in-law's involvement in a federal terrorist watchlist lawsuit, days before former President Barack Obama campaigns with him.
articles.body: Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged Saturday night that his sister-in-law was involved in a federal terrorist watchlist lawsuit during the Obama administration, just days before former President Barack Obama is scheduled to campaign alongside him. El-Sayed was confronted by Fox News senior correspondent Mike Tobin about court documents identifying his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, as a plaintiff in a 2016 lawsuit challenging her alleged placement on the federal Terrorism Screening Database, commonly known as the terrorist watchlist. "There's reporting in a lawsuit that now backs it up. And documentation with the lawsuit that Mariam Jukaku, who's your sister-in-law, that she was on the terrorist watch list?" Tobin asked. "Yeah," El-Sayed responded. MICHIGAN SENATE DEBATE ERUPTS INTO PERSONAL ATTACKS AS ROGERS, EL-SAYED CLASH OVER ISRAEL, IRAN AND MORE El-Sayed then defended his sister-in-law, insisting she had committed no wrongdoing and turning his criticism toward Republican Senate rival Mike Rogers. "She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off," El-Sayed said. "You've got this system where folks are guilty until proven innocent because they've got different kinds of names, because of the infrastructure that people like Mike Rogers set up." The exchange comes as Obama prepares to campaign alongside El-Sayed in Michigan on Oct. 24, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election. EL-SAYED ASKED IF HE BELIEVES AMERICA IS 'READY FOR A MUSLIM PRESIDENT' AHEAD OF SENATE RACE According to the 2016 complaint, Jukaku underwent additional airport screening in 2012, and alleged she was never told why she had been flagged. The filing said she was believed to have been removed from the watchlist by 2016. El-Sayed said she sued and won, but a federal appeals court overturned a ruling favoring the plaintiffs in 2021. A separate lawsuit seeking damages was dismissed in 2017. Despite El-Sayed's claim that she sued and won, a federal appeals court overturned a ruling favoring the plaintiffs in 2021, while a separate lawsuit seeking damages was dismissed in 2017. TRUMP LINKS MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD: 'HE'S A CON MAN' The FBI said it does not confirm or deny individuals' watchlist status. "It is the U.S. government’s policy to neither confirm nor deny a person’s inclusion in the Terrorist Screening Dataset, commonly known as the terrorist watchlist," the agency told Fox News. The exchange follows separate allegations about El-Sayed's family's purported Muslim Brotherhood connections, which his campaign called "racist and untrue." Rogers called the allegations "disqualifying" Saturday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The watchlist lawsuit does not establish wrongdoing by Jukaku or El-Sayed.

articles.title: Shapiro launches super PAC as presidential speculation mounts
articles.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) is launching a new political action committee (PAC), raising speculation that the governor may run for president in 2028. The committee, called New Path PAC, says on its website that it is dedicated to electing candidates who will oppose President Trump. “New Path PAC will help Governor Josh Shapiro build…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) is launching a new political action committee (PAC), raising speculation that the governor may run for president in 2028.

The committee, called New Path PAC , says on its website that it is dedicated to electing candidates who will oppose President Trump.

“New Path PAC will help Governor Josh Shapiro build a movement to get citizens to rise up, demand more, and elect candidates who will put a check on Donald Trump and JD Vance’s chaos, cruelty, and corruption,” the website says.

Shapiro is considered one of many potential presidential candidates for Democrats in 2028. His popularity in Pennsylvania — a Quinnipiac University poll earlier this month found his job approval at 62 percent — has raised his stock among some in the party.

But first, Shapiro has to win reelection, with polls consistently showing he has a comfortable lead.

The Quinnipiac poll put him ahead of his Republican opponent by 26 points, 60 percent to 34 percent, among likely voters. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Shapiro a 95 percent chance of winning reelection.

But even in his gubernatorial campaign, Shapiro is already receiving questions about his future ambitions. In an Oct. 7 debate against his Republican opponent Stacy Garrity, the Pennsylvania state treasurer, moderators asked Shapiro whether he would commit to serving his full four-year term as governor if he is reelected in November.

Instead of answering directly, Shapiro said that Garrity would not finish her term as treasurer if she were to win the governor’s race.

“The treasurer made a commitment she would serve her full term as treasurer,” Shapiro said. “She’s obviously broken that, and I’m going to do everything in my power to ensure she’s able to serve all four years.”

When asked in the past if he will run for president, Shapiro has not answered the question directly. But he told Rev. Al Sharpton at a convention in April that he will “be a part of” conversations about the party’s future.

articles.title: No Kings rallies across U.S. urge voters to cast ballots early in the midterms
articles.summary: Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.
articles.body: Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections. The hundreds of planned events were billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency. A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” were among the many signs held aloft. At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. “The Constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” he said. “You don’t see Superman giving up his power,” Bond continued. “You don’t see Black Panther giving up his power. You don’t see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote.” Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election. His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. On Friday the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. Earlier that day Democratic Sens. Alex Padilla of California, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Dick Durbin of Illinois wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.
